11 Climber Gift Ideas You Probably Haven’t Thought of Yet, According to Editors

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1432 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

Industry observers note that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

(Photo: L to R: Anthony Walsh, Etsy Glass Carabiner Shop, Metolius, Yosemite Climbing Association, Kong).

If you’ve already taken a lap through our gift guide and still need more ideas, we’ve got you. All three of us editors here at Climbing have selected our top picks for gifts this year, from gear we’ve got our eyes on, to accessories in the climbing zeitgeist right now.

Some of these editor gifts picks make perfect mini gifts for stocking stuffers or for that climber partner who you want to thank for giving you the perfect soft catch this past year. Other picks make a bigger impact, from a super lightweight harness to a great gym bag. Most of our picks are great for a variety of climbers, whether it’s your fresh boyfriend who you hope to convert into a climber, or your mentor who’s been at it for eons.

We hope these gift ideas make your holiday shopping as painless as a splitter hand crack so you can spend more time training or climbing, and less time scrolling through endless product pages and catalogs.

Sources indicate that originally designed and hand-sewn by Nate Barton—the Missoula-based climber who ran the meme account @beta.sprayer until 2024—the Lolo Hoodie V1 ($169.99) is a functional midlayer for cold-weather climbing and the flagship product of the fledgling brand Lolo Hardware. Its large, zippered chest pocket was originally intended to help ice climbers warm up their hands between pitches.

It has been revealed that having pretty much lived in this hoodie for the past three winters, I’ve found the chest pocket far superior to any sort of pant pocket for storing my phone, gloves, and snacks. Plus, with my items against my chest, I never have to worry about my phone freezing or my car keys accidentally slipping out during a chimney. From Joshua Tree in January to Canyonlands in November, this is a comfy and durable hoodie for the coldest days and nights of climbing.

It’s 2026, folks: If you’re still using mined chalk instead of seawater-sourced chalk, this is your call to finally make the switch. Climbing’s feature on the hidden environmental impact of chalk showed how the vast majority of magnesium carbonate comes from mines in China, where magnesite factories poison the water and soil of nearby residents.

It has been revealed that luckily, there are plenty of sustainable brands that produce seawater-sourced chalk by using solar power to evaporate ocean brine from seawater. Here are some of our favorites:.

Shop Midnight Lightning Sea Grip Liquid Chalk.

According to recent reports, for climbers with pierced ears, a pair of carabiner earrings is a customizable accessory that never gets old. Recently, I’ve been getting tons of compliments on my pair of silver, locker draw earrings (yes, they actually screw and unscrew!) that I bought at the Yosemite Climbing Museum in July. You can buy them here, but stock is limited. In case they sell out, here are a few other great places to buy carabiner earrings online:.

It has been revealed that after breaking a cross-loaded carabiner in a scary trad fall, I now always add some sort of tape or rubber band to keep cam carabiners in place. I wrote about my DIY solution a couple of years ago, but now I simply slide on Avant Climbing’s Flip-Stop Cam Carabiner Stabilizers ($22.50 for a 10-pack). The Flip-Stop makes for easy cam clipping when mega pumped. But unlike my rubber band hack, it also keeps the cam sling open for clipping a long draw into. Crucially, like a quickdraw’s dogbone, the Flip-Stop prevents carabiners from rotating onto the dangerously weak X-axis. Nothing ruins the holidays like a pair of broken ankles.

The fresh Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness ($180) may weigh less than the gift wrap paper you’ll hide it in. At an absurdly light 78 grams (2.7oz), the Alpha SL is for those going ultralight in the mountains, whether that’s an alpine rock romp or a big ski traverse. This harness is also surprisingly comfortable to rappel in, thanks to its uber-stiff Aluula-composite construction. And it fits a range of body types thanks to its adjustable leg loops and five waistbelt sizes. Just don’t set it down unattended on a glacier—it’ll blow away in the slightest gust of wind.

Shop Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness.

The Patagonia Airshed Pro Pullover ($169) might have been built for mountain running, but I wear mine year-round on all sorts of objectives, from sunny rock climbs to cold north faces. The Airshed Pro is a pseudo-windlayer: decently breathable for high-output activities, yet stills blocks the wind and has a water-repellent coating. The result is a shirt equally at home skiing on a glacier or rambling up a gusty rock ridge.

Sources indicate that A note on sizing: Since the Airshed Pro was originally designed for runners, the cut is quite slim. I size up to facilitate a wider range of motion.

In a recent development, I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody ($299) as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air.

Industry observers note that the pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack without a cam or crampon tearing into the insulation. I’m also looking forward to using this as a mid-layer below a shell for ice climbing this winter.

In a recent development, unless you’ve been living under a rock (which many of our readers hopefully have), you’ve heard about the upcoming film about the weed plane that crashed into a Yosemite lake in 1976. What followed was a tragicomic climber gold rush. Now, to mark the 50th anniversary of the incident, you can sport one of several new t-shirts or hats ($29.95-$44.95) memorializing this infamous moment in Yosemite climbing history. All proceeds support the Yosemite Climbing Association and the Yosemite Climbing Museum.

Have I used one? No. Do I desperately want one? Yes. As a 5’2” climber, I’m often just a few inches short of being able to make the clip from a good stance. I’ve heard wonderful things about the stiffy Kong Panic Draw ($54.95-$59.95) that lets you clip bolts otherwise out of reach. Maybe 2027 will be the year I finally gift myself one! If there’s a short or easily panicked sport climber in your life, I bet they would be stoked to get this as a present. Or you could make one for them DIY-style yourself.

In a recent development, the oversized, durable Metolius Climbers Tote ($64.95) has become my go-to gym bag. It easily fits my personal gear plus a 60m rope, or four sets of personal gear (shoes, harness, and chalkbag for me, my husband, and my two kids). Despite having stored weathered climbing shoes zippered inside for too long, this bag miraculously doesn’t stink yet either. It stows away nicely in gym cubbies (whereas my previous Cotopaxi tote would sort of spill out) and is easy to carry by hand or shoulder. This is a great mid-sized gift for the climber in your life, or you could fill it with other gear you’re gifting for a bigger impact.

Industry observers note that note on price: While this tote isn’t on sale at REI, co-op members get 20% off one full-price item through Nov. 30, so this is a good one to save on.

It has been revealed that I receive a lot of climbing books and galleys to review and consider for coverage. Only some of them are so good that I can’t put them down. That’s how I felt about Erratica, a fresh collection of true stories from Moab-based, life-long climber Brian Laidlaw. Rare is the read that both keeps you attentive and entertained, yet also evokes deeper reflection. With Erratica, Brian manages to do just that. Pick up a copy ($20) at Moab’s Back of Beyond bookstore, or find one online anywhere books are sold.

Midnight Lightning Sea Grip Liquid Chalk.

Latest Update: A Climber We Lost: Jun Kyu Kim

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On August 21, 2026, Jun Kyu Kim was scrambling on the approach to a climb in Eldorado Canyon, when he fell.
  • It has been revealed that born on April 3, 1981, Jun was raised by his loving parents Hyoun Sook Kim and Ho Young Kim, and grew up in Chicago with his two sisters.
  • Jun once stated that climbing was the thing he lived for.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy Gisely Ferraz).

On August 21, 2026, Jun Kyu Kim was scrambling on the approach to a climb in Eldorado Canyon, when he fell. Even though he was wearing a helmet, he suffered a fatal head injury. The tragedy shook the Denver climbing community he had been a part of. Jun touched so many lives, whether through Cruxing in Color, of which he was an early supporter, or at the crag, where he was known to offer kind advice and encouraging words. He leaves behind his loving family, his girlfriend, and so many friends whose lives were made better by his generosity and kindness.

It has been revealed that born on April 3, 1981, Jun was raised by his loving parents Hyoun Sook Kim and Ho Young Kim, and grew up in Chicago with his two sisters. Throughout his life, Jun was known for his adventurous spirit and zest for exploration. He discovered his love for the outdoors—where he found peace and joy—at an early age during a National Outdoor Leadership School trip to Alaska. It was during high school that he was introduced to rock climbing, which quickly became his true passion.

Jun once stated that climbing was the thing he lived for. In the climbing community, he was known for his trademark red hat, dirtbag clothes, love for donuts, and his patented naps. He could sleep anytime and anywhere, then upon waking, send his project. After completing a route, he’d often be out like a light. Ever a favorite climbing partner, he exuded confidence, patience, and calm under pressure. And he settled people’s nerves, allowing them to achieve ever harder things. When friends would get down on themselves about their climbing, he was always the first to remind them to not take climbing so seriously, to have fun, and to give themselves grace on high gravity days.

I spoke with Jun’s girlfriend, Sz-min Harley, and his best friend, Shawnee, to learn more about what Jun meant to the people he climbed with. Many people saw him as a mentor. He would frequently take less experienced climbers under his wing. But he also was famous for sandbagging. If you accepted his suggestion, you knew you could be in for a far more difficult adventure than you had counted on. But Jun’s encouraging words, infectious laughter, and love for fun would make it all worth the story in the end. Shawnee notes that the first time they climbed together was in El Salto, where he had Shawnee try his warm-up. She could barely get halfway up before she had to come down. Jun refused to tell Shawnee the grade, but she later found out it was a 5.12b.

Sources indicate that jun was also known for his love of cooking, something that he learned from his mom at a young age. He continued to cook with her until the end. For Jun, food was a love language. He liked few things better than bringing people together around a meal, whether in the kitchen or around a campfire. The first time he came to visit Shawnee, he drove six hours and indicated up with a cooler full of homemade Korean dishes for her to try. Once, he cooked dinner for the 20 people who had signed up for his friends’ newly debuted Beyond Jamming crack climbing clinic in Indian Creek. The entire crew came back from a full day of climbing, tired and hungry, to a grinning Jun. He had made homemade tacos for everyone, complete with vegetarian, gluten-free, and lactose-free options.

That was Jun—a man with an unbelievably major heart who was always looking for a way to help and who showed up every day for his friends. He was the kind of friend who would always be there for you, whether you needed a belay on a project or a partner willing to head out to that route tucked away in a far corner of the desert. Never letting the friendship fade, Jun was known for checking in on the people he loved, making sure you knew that he was thinking of you. He would help fix your van, make you chicken soup when you were sick, and send you a card just to say he was glad you existed. Not only did Jun give love from the bottom of his heart, but he did it without expecting anything in return.

In a recent development, jun’s friend Adien shared something that has stuck with me: “Jun was a rare, selfless climber. He would go to the crag for himself, but he would go for you.”.

According to recent reports, climbing took Jun all over the world—Thailand, Greece, Columbia, Cuba, Chile, Mexico. But until the end, his favorite place was always Indian Creek. The first time he went, he and a friend only had four cams that they bumped up the routes, bearing miserably cold weather. Yet, the Creek still managed to claim his heart. Over the years, that love became even stronger and more special. Season after season, he made memories of hard sends, campfires, and laughter with his friends. For those who loved him, the Creek will never be the same.

Forty five years around the sun would never be enough, but Jun managed to fill those years with more life than most people do in twice as much time.

We miss you, Jun, and we will always carry you with us, keeping your spirit alive by choosing generosity, connection, and care.

Some people book a luxury hotel for the weekend. Others would rather throw a tent in the car and figure out where they’re sleeping later. If you have one of the latter on your holiday shopping list, we’ve got you covered. Below are the best camping gifts that will make their time outside a bit more comfortable—even if they swear they don’t care about that. From the practical gear they’ll use on every trip to the fun extras that let them have their creature comforts, these presents will have them plotting their getaway ASAP.

Industry observers note that A good pair of hiking socks is always appreciated, but these come with a little extra feel-good factor. Made with 70 percent organic cotton and a cushioned footbed, Conscious Step socks are comfortable enough for long days on the trail (or lazy ones around camp). Even better, purchases support the National Parks Conservation Association, which works to protect America’s public lands.

This interactive water bottle doubles as an excuse to proposal their next substantial camping trip. It comes with 63 illustrated, water-resistant stickers representing every national park in the U.S., so they can track where they’ve visited as they go. Since it’s a Nalgene, it’s also durable and featherlight, perfect for hanging from backpacks and gear bags.

This is the ideal gift for the person who considers coffee a nonnegotiable, regardless of how far they’ve wandered from civilization. This compact brewer is roughly the size of a thermos and makes hot coffee and cold brew concentrate in minutes. Simply add finely ground coffee and hot or cold water, let it brew, then use the hand press to dispense a concentrated shot into the included carafe. With no plugs and no charging required, they can throw it in their bag and go.

Camp chairs are great, but they’re not always the easiest things to lug around. This compact stool weighs just 1.2 pounds, folds down to 7.5 inches, and has a swiveling seat that lets you turn without having to pick up and reposition the whole thing. It supports up to 260 pounds, too, which is impressive for its size.

It has been revealed that this is a particularly useful piece of gear for any camper who wants to cut down on what they’re carrying. Hydrapak’s collapsible flask has a built-in filter that removes common waterborne bacteria and parasites, allowing hikers to refill from water sources along the trail. It weighs just 4.1 ounces and packs completely flat when empty. It’s a great option for biking, hiking, paddling, and even traveling through sketchy airport bathrooms.

A headlamp is one of those camping essentials you don’t fully appreciate until you’re stumbling around camp in the dark. The Storm delivers up to 550 lumens with adjustable brightness, three different colored modes (red, blue, and green) to preserve night vision, and a waterproof-rated IPX7 construction that can handle rain and snow. It also has a lock mode to prevent it from accidentally turning on in your pack and draining the batteries before you even reach camp.

Sources indicate that if you want your family and friends to experience comfort in camp, look no further than this hammock. The kit has everything someone needs to set up between two trees, including polyester straps and iron carabiners. The Portable Hammock has a weight capacity of 551 pounds and it exhibits both the toughness and user-friendliness that Jeep is known for: It’s made from durable nylon and conveniently packs away into a built-in pouch that doubles as a pocket when the hammock is set up.

According to recent reports, there are hundreds of camp slippers on the market, but few are as truly warm or versatile as Glerups. Made from 100 percent natural wool, they’re naturally temperature-regulating and odor-resistant, so feet stay comfortable without getting swampy. The slip-on design makes them easy to kick off tent-side, while the rubber sole handles dirt, mud, and slippery moss with ease.

Finicky sleepers will love this sleeping bag. The Kelty Eclipse skips the traditional zipper in favor of a clever wraparound design that campers spread out when they’re hot or cocoon themself when they’re cold. What it lacks in zippers it makes up for in thoughtful details, including a self-sealing foot vent, oversized hood to keep pillows in place, and internal pockets. It’s also rated to 15 degrees Fahrenheit, so it’s built for more than just balmy summer nights.

It has been revealed that A good outdoor blanket earns its keep in just about every situation, and Yeti’s Lowlands is designed to handle more than one night under the stars. Its waterproof, puncture-resistant bottom keeps damp ground from seeping through, while the cushioned top provides a comfortable place to sit, stretch out, or let the dog settle in. Roll it up for transport, then bring it out for everything from picnics to beach days to tailgates.

It has been revealed that if their cooking kit is just a recycled takeout container and one random spork, please get them this Gerber set. The 16-piece set includes a saute pan, stock pot, hot pad, and tableware for four people, giving them everything they need to make and serve a proper meal without cobbling together a kitchen from mismatched gear. When they’re finished, everything nests together for easy packing until the next time they need it.

These are the pants they’ll put on once at camp and have absolutely no interest in taking off, especially in colder temps. The Fernos pair a cozy insulated interior with a water-resistant exterior, making them ideal for chilly mornings, lounging around the campsite, or layering over a base layer when snow starts to fall. In other words, they’re very durable sweatpants.

This is about as close as campers can get to bringing their mattress into the woods. The 3.9-inch memory foam pad is thick, supportive, and genuinely comfortable—more proper bed than half-deflated sleeping pad situation. It’s not designed for backpacking (don’t try to carry this on a thru-hike), but it’s portable enough to toss in the car for weekend camping trips. It rolls up tightly for storage and transport and self-inflates when unrolled, making set-up a breeze.

Recent findings suggest that one of the best things about Luno’s car camping mattresses is that they’re not reserved for people with tricked-out 4x4s. The Air Pro is designed to fit a wide range of vehicles, with custom-fit options for dozens of makes and models. This particular kit includes a luxe inflatable mattress, air pump, fitted sheet, pillow, and window screen set that turns their backseat into a dreamy place to sleep. Simply put in their car’s year, make, and model and choose their window size for the gift of spontaneous overnights and long road trips.

It has been revealed that this is for the camp chef who thinks camping dinner should involve way more than hot dogs and s’mores. The Gozney Tread is a portable pizza oven that heats up to 950°F and cooks a delicious pie in about a minute. Its compact design makes it shockingly easy to transport and it runs on propane, so they won’t need to fuss with building a fire. Sure, it’s a bit of a splurge for the campsite, but the lucky recipient will have no trouble convincing their camping buddies it’s worth the extra trunk space.

All campers know that a tent you can properly stand up in is the gift that keeps on giving. The Aurora Highrise has near-vertical walls and a roomy interior that comfortably accommodates up to six people, making it a good pick for families or groups who don’t love sleeping elbow-to-elbow. How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

  • According to recent reports, so if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area. There are a few reasons for this. One is that permadraws are highly visible, turning a natural setting into an outdoor climbing gym. Permadraws also corrode rapidly in marine and coastal environments. Lastly, they are expensive.

According to recent reports, so if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route? Leaving a carabiner is the next easiest solution. But what if you don’t want to do that?

According to recent reports, these nagging questions—as well as recent accidents—have compelled me to put together this long list of options for cleaning your next steep line. I’ve organized these methods into three categories:.

Each method has pros and cons in regards to simplicity, speed, and safety.

Ultimately, no single “best method” exists. Though there is a singular worst method: rappelling. Cleaning steep routes on rappel is a huge hassle for the climber, and bystanders on the ground who inevitably have to assist. Your method of choice will come down to the circumstances of each route and your personal preferences on simplicity, speed, and risk tolerance. Many of these methods are best saved for niche scenarios, or rare “if-then” situations. Still, it is best to be prepared with knowledge and equipment for those odd cleaning scenarios.

In a recent development, below, I will discuss several methods for cleaning on the way up. I choose this approach if a route has a roof or dangerous swing potential or if, for whatever reason, I’m not ready to clean the route on the way down. Cleaning on the way up can take more time, but it brings safety gains. Methods range from simple to complex. If cleaning on the way down looks like a nuisance, just lower down to the ground and deal with it later (i.e., on the way back up).

Sources indicate that if the route is well within the abilities of someone in your party, toproping to clean is always a good go-to. Never turn down a free toprope, right?

Recent findings suggest that concerns with this method arise when the climbing gets hard enough where the climber might fall on toprope, thus becoming stuck in space. If the climber is unable to get back to the wall and decides to lower, then you may end up needing to re-lead the climb to re-clip the draws/directionals, so someone can attempt cleaning on toprope again. This is a huge pain, but I see it very often. Thankfully, there are many methods that can help you avoid this scenario.

Firstly, when someone is toproping to clean, we always say they must promise to get to the top. That way, they won’t leave the rope unclipped from lifesaving directionals. This reminder helps incentivize the climber to “blueprint falls.” The worst time to fall is immediately after unclipping a bolt, when the swing will be the farthest, potentially leaving the climber stranded. If you think you might fall, it’s best to adequately rest hanging at a bolt before unclipping. Only unclip the bolt once you’re ready to charge to the next one.

What if you get unlucky and fall into space? You can try pulling on the belayer’s end of the rope if it’s within reach. However, this method is usually much less productive on steep topropes than on steep lead climbs. Oftentimes, pulling on the rope will get you nowhere.

If pulling on the rope is getting you nowhere, the next method is boinking. Usually performed on lead, boinking is a strategy a leader can employ after falling into space and becoming unable to reach the rock or a rope. But it does work (albeit sometimes less effectively) on toprope. It’s also tiring and best for short stretches.

Industry observers note that the boinking method is simple, but often executed inefficiently. The belayer takes tight on the rope, ideally, and hovers above the ground, or over an edge where they can hang their full body weight. Then, the climber does a pull-up on the climber side of the rope to create a loop of slack. When the climber rapidly releases the slack, the belayer drops. If the belayer is too low to the ground, they will hit the ground, and usually blame the climber.

It has been revealed that for maximum efficiency, the belayer can easily ascend the rope (using an ascender and their Grigri) the same distance that the climber needs to ascend. This obviates the need for timing the boinking/drops and is far more relaxing for both parties. It’s also far more efficient than the belayer jumping to take at the right time.

Industry observers note that an alternative to boinking is climbing the leash, as it’s called by highliners. This is the main method highliners use to climb the leash after falling, but also works identically in climbing scenarios when you’re not too far below your clip. If you’re flexible, place your heel above your tie-in knot, then pull on the rope, until you can straighten your leg and reach high for the wall. Once you pull on the wall or a draw, the belayer must rapidly take in all the extra slack.

Have the aforementioned methods become too tiring or inefficient? Or is there too much rope drag or rope stretch in the system for them to be effective? The next method is for the stuck climber to ascend the rope. If I don’t want to do the climbing again, I’ll usually jump straight to this method since I always have an ascender with me at the crag. If it’s just a short section to ascend, a prusik or other autoblock will work fine. But for cleaning a full route, you’ll thank yourself for bringing a proper ascender or at least nano-trax, to the crag (they weigh nothing).

If it is too difficult to pull in and release a draw, you can relocate your ascender above the draw, then clip a PAS/draw into the top carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. Slack the rope from your Grigri to unclip the rope from the draw. If you forgot to move the ascender above the clip, it will get stuck here. Begin ascending again until there is a 90-degree angle between your PAS and tensioned rope. The closer this angle is to 90 degrees, the less muscle required to pull in and unclip the draw. When you unclip the draw from the bolt, it stays attached to your PAS as you go swinging.

Sometimes rope shenanigans can get a bit clunky, especially in roofs. If the bolts are close enough together, you can implement some aid climbing techniques as needed. Sometimes it’s easier to ascend via yarding on bolts, and top-stepping in slings than jugging when it’s really steep. Just do whatever it takes to get up there and reclaim those draws! This can be done in a toprope scenario or a jugging scenario, with a slacked rope, or tensioned.

In a recent development, the biggest error when cleaning steep routes is cleaning on the way down, then taking a dangerous swing low on the route. There are many ways to clean on the way down. We’ll start with the standard scenario, then dive into niche techniques for oddball scenarios.

Many routes have an anchor just below the steep climbing. If this is the case, once you finish cleaning the steep terrain, the first step is to go off belay at that anchor and untie. Then pull the rope from above, re-tie in, and re-lower. When bolting routes, I love adding this type of anchor, not only to provide an easier, shorter version of the route, but also to greatly simplify the process of cleaning lower down the route.

The most common method for cleaning a steep sport route while lowering is to employ a trolley draw (it goes by many names). This draw connects the belay loop to the belayer’s side of the rope. As you lower, you can pull in on the belayer’s line to clean the draws. Higher up on the route, call for your belayer to hold (stop lowering) when the rope below your trolley draw is nearly level. Lower down on the route, you’ll want to stop sooner, just above the bolt.

There are a few methods for retrieving the draws, but whatever you do, be sure to stop and think before unclipping anything.

It has been revealed that the quickest method is to simply grab the wall, pull in (not up) to slack the draw and remove the draw from the bolt. If you can’t grab holds, often you can draw dyno: grab the draw with two hands and thrust in (not up) to momentarily slack the draw to remove it. In either of these cases, it is far more strenuous to remove the rope from the draw since your trolley draw will be yanking you away from the wall when you still have to clean the draw from the bolt. TLDR: If you’re tensioning the trolley, unclip the draw from the bolt.

Recent findings suggest that if those methods aren’t working, go in direct to the draw you are hoping to retrieve. You can clip your PAS directly to the top carabiner of the draw. If using a draw to go direct, clip an additional draw from the belay loop to the lower carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. It’s best to resist the temptation to relocate the trolley draw into a tether draw. Note that if you remove your trolley draw and do not replace it, you could later unexpectedly fall into space or take a dangerous swing.

Recent findings suggest that once you’ve clipped direct to the draw, you can unclip the rope from the draw you wish to clean, calling slack if needed. Now, unlike other methods, the primary tension is no longer on the trolley, but instead directly on the bolt. Now pull down on the belayer’s rope to assist them in taking. That 90-degree rule applies here, too. Double check that your trolley is in place, assess the swing potential, then remove the draw from the bolt, and take the swing.

Industry observers note that the lower you go on the route, the more potential energy—and extra rope—builds up in the system. If the trolley accidentally comes unclipped for any reason, it can be catastrophic. You could swing and hit a rock or a tree. The extra rope could even cause you to hit the ground. For this reason, as I get lower, I’ll often double-up my trolley draw. Why not?

Industry observers note that now let’s imagine we’ve lowered all the way down to the first bolt. As mentioned, the farther we end up from the plumb line, the higher the potential swing risk. Sometimes it is safe to unclip and take the swing. Other times, you might hit trees, rocks, or the ground. If both parties decide the swing is safe, the climber must first unclip the trolley draw before taking the swing. If you forget to unclip the trolley draw, you’ll drag the belayer along the ground as you swing. Very unpleasant!

Recent findings suggest that if the belayer is firmly anchored you can opt to keep the trolley draw in place to minimize the swing. However, since most sport crags don’t have convenient ground anchors, this option isn’t always possible. Just remember, don’t expect your belayer alone to stop your swing!

It has been revealed that if you’re unsure whether a swing is safe, it’s usually best not to risk it. The horizontal distance of a swing is only a small part of understanding the potential impact. A giant King Swing can be perfectly safe, while a seemingly harmless three-foot swing can be devastating. The greater the starting angle of the swing, the more gravitational potential energy the climber has.

According to recent reports, once past the rope’s vertical plumb line (the lowest point of the swing), the climber begins losing speed. However, impact force depends just as much on how abruptly the climber is stopped as it does on their speed. Finally, account for rope stretch, which can increase the swing’s radius and lower the climber’s trajectory. Always make sure your swing won’t put you into the ground or another obstacle!

Even if the swing is all air, there can still be a risk of sharp rock cutting the rope. For this reason, it’s best to avoid major swings if the rope is rubbing rock. Usually, it’s the swing back toward the wall where rope damage is most likely to occur. Ropes cut most commonly from sideways grinding or sliding. If the rope must press rock, I prefer to place the rope where the rock is perpendicular to the rope’s force.

If a swing looks risky, the safest and easiest thing is to leave a draw or a carabiner. In my 20-plus years of sport climbing, I’ve never left a carabiner, but I do love this method because it’s allowed me to collect hundreds of free carabiners over the years, which I repurpose as lower-offs on anchors.

According to recent reports, besides cost, there are additional downsides to leaving gear. It is annoying to clip a bolt that has a bail carabiner. Numerous reported accidents exist wherein a climber falls after clipping a draw to the hanger over an existing carabiner, causing the draw’s carabiner to break. For this reason, people climbing after you should hopefully know to slide their draw between the carabiner and the wall when clipping.

In a recent development, on coastal routes, solid gate carabiners will eventually corrode shut, requiring a saw to remove. On the coast, only leave wiregates unless the wall is frequently trafficked. Speaking of difficult to remove, quick links should not be left on lead bolts. They require someone else to stop their climbing to use two hands to clean up after you. They are not cheaper than carabiners, unless you use the cheap hardware store ones that rust over and eventually require a saw to remove. If you must leave something, it must be a carabiner. Buy a stick clip and you’ll get an endless supply of free carabiners!

Let’s say we’ve decided to leave a draw. Now just stay connected with your trolley and continue lowering to the ground. The system will experience extra friction with the zigzag in the rope, which is nice. If you want to leave just a carabiner, you’ll go in direct to the draw you wish to clean, slack the rope, and clip the carabiner to the bolt above the draw. Then insert the climber’s end of the rope to the carabiner. Take hard, then remove the draw, and lower.

With both of these methods, you can still retrieve your draw/carabiner. The fastest, and sketchiest way to do so is to solo up to the first bolt (and back down). If it’s easy climbing and you’re comfortable, it does get the job done swiftly. Otherwise, removing the draw with a stick clip is much safer, and won’t take too much longer.

Now let’s dig into a couple specialized scenarios.

Technically, the advice that follows on reclaiming the quickdraw from the first bolt safely is part of cleaning a route on the way down. But it involves some niche skills. So, let’s imagine you don’t want to leave a carabiner or draw behind on the first bolt. And you also don’t want to solo up to the first bolt, nor do you have a stick clip. If it’s a massive, rounded glue-in, you can do a lower-out off the first bolt. In short, a lower-out is using a length of rope to do a secondary lower that safely equalizes the climber onto the plumb line. The goal here is to cancel out the swing potential, not to lower to the ground, so the belayer should hold tight. Do not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete or you’ll use up more rope on the lower-out than expected.

Industry observers note that there are several ways to set up a lower-out. My favorite method? Give myself a huge tail on a figure-8 on a bight when cleaning the anchor. I make that tail double the length of the distance from the bolt to the object I might hit on a swing. When I arrive at that bolt, I go in direct. Then I unclip the trolley and ask my belayer to relocate under the anchor so they don’t swing. Once they’ve taken hard, I pass the extra long tail through the bolt, tension the extra tail, unclip my attachment to the bolt, lower myself out, then pull the rope through the bolt.

In a recent development, lower-outs can be done with a knot on the end of the lower-out strand or without. Remember, you should always have the knot in the end of the belayer’s strand! Having a knot on the lower-out chord can keep you from lowering off the end and taking a bad swing if the chord comes up short. However, other times, skipping the knot can sometimes be safer (more on that in a minute). This is where stopping and analyzing is important.

Lower-outs can be done with and without a belay device. If it is a pure roof or horizontal traverse, I will use a belay device to lower-out as the forces are significant. This also puts a lot of friction (wear and tear) on the hangers, and should be done sparingly. If the angle is less extreme, I often prefer to lower-out by hand without a belay device. With this method, it is absolutely imperative that the belayer does not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete. Otherwise, the force on your hands will go from very comfortable to dangerous.

But, why on earth would I ever prefer not using a belay device? If your lower-out chord is a tad short, finishing the lower-out by hand is often necessary to maximize your reach before letting go of the chord. The most dangerous option is to use a belay device and no knot; the glitch being that it is very difficult to lower without your back facing the wall you’re trying to avoid hitting. Additionally, transitioning from lowering with the device to lowering by hand is risky. The safest thing is to knot the end, lower-out with an assisted braking belay device, hang on the device to clear the knot, then finish lowering by hand. If the pendulum angle is mild enough, I’ll skip those first steps and lower the whole way by hand.

If you use the lower-out method, make sure you have extra rope, as well as a knot in the belayer’s end of the rope. I’d recommend practicing lower-outs in no-risk scenarios first to understand the forces. You may be surprised how easy and safe it can be to two-hand the rope. After the lower-out, simply pull the rope to retrieve. If the belayer avoids lowering during the lower-out, the rope friction on the bolt is minimal and wear and tear on the bolt is non-existent. Still, it’s better to avoid making a habit out of this.

It has been revealed that but what if it’s not a fat rounded glue-in bolt? In that case, I’d highly recommend against a lower-out due to the rubbing of the rope on the sharper hanger. In this case, I would do a rappel-out. You’d rig it the same as a lower-out, but you set up your extra tail as a rappel instead of a lower (find the midpoint of your tail). Similarly, the belayer must avoid the temptation to lower.

In a recent development, while you are rappelling out, negligible rope pressure exists on the hanger, but you won’t create any tensioned rubbing friction like you would when lowering. When equalized onto the plumb line, you can pull the rope through the bolt hanger just like before. To further lessen any friction of the rope on the hanger while pulling, flick the tail and pull when the rope is lightest. This way, there will be no wear and tear.

Let’s say you weren’t planning to do a lower-out or rappel-out. Your belayer can toss you the bottom of the lead line to use just the same. Just make sure that before you untie the stopper knot at the end of the line, that the belayer ties a newly introduced stopper knot on their break strand (an overhand on a bight is fine). This requires a bit more rope than the first method, so just be careful.

But what if we don’t have enough rope for a lower-out and you don’t have the means to retrieve the draw any other way? If the bolt is solid, you can rappel straight through the bolt hanger. Blasphemy! This is clearly a last resort, but if you’re going to do it, you should at least know the best method. Firstly, never lower through a bolt hanger. That creates much more friction on the rope and bolt than a lower-out or pulling the rope after rappelling.

I personally do not believe pulling the rope after rappelling would cause any wear and tear, especially if it is a fatty rounded glue-in. What about an expansion bolt’s hanger? Recent tests have shown this scenario to hold around 11kN. There is some mild risk to the rope when pulling it due to the sharper edges. Just like the rappel-out, you can flick the end of the rope and pull the rope when it’s lightest. Additionally, having minimal extra rope to pull through the bolt is key. Rig the rope so its end barely touches the ground.

Lastly, avoid this technique above 15-20 feet off the ground unless it’s an emergency scenario because the rope weight will cause more friction when pulling. And of course, this can all be avoided with a stick clip.

Recent findings suggest that if the bolts are close enough together, it’s often easier to just down-aid the route. The steeper the route, the less I’ll tension the rope. In a full roof with close enough bolts, I won’t tension the rope at all. There’s no need for bulky aiders though. I like to keep a 120cm sling coiled up on a lightweight carabiner permanently on my harness, using draws as a PAS.

Sources indicate that if the route involves a full roof, it’s usually best to just down-lead/back-aid the route. This is the standard method with the massive roof cracks in Canyonlands. If you can bump cams then there’s no need to tension the rope.

It has been revealed that however, this article is about sport climbing. What do you do in a pure roof with spaced out bolts? After running into this scenario many times, I find it easier to do a mix of toprope to clean and jugging the rope. I leave my Grigri on the rope, while the belayer belays with their Grigri, sometimes taking in slack, and sometimes acting as a meat anchor. A Black Diamond grappling hook on the bolt hanger allows me to easily unhook the bolt and take the swing.

Speaking of getting creative, let’s wrap up with what will likely be one of the more controversial takes in this article. I’ve often found the fastest, safest (if you pay attention), and easiest (overall for the team) method is for the climber and belayer to both clean simultaneously. I can’t outright recommend it, unless you have a great attention to detail and years of experience with all of the previous techniques, as well as a variety of other techniques. But I’m including it for those climbing veterans who want to help their partners clean faster and easier.

I generally jump to this method if cleaning the lower part of the route on the way down would be a nuisance or dangerous, but cleaning the top on lower is no-problem. First, I tie off the brake strand on my Grigri. Then, in order to lower the climber, I will climb up the route. I go up, they go down. In doing so, they cancel out much of my weight. If the climbing is hard, I’ll just jug up to the first bolt, clip in, and lower them to their next bolt. We both clean our respective bolts at our leisure. The only communication needed is for the climber to call the standard, “lower” and “hold.”.

Recent findings suggest that the climber should stop cleaning one bolt before (above) entering any dangerous swing potential. Once they’ve hit that point, they just hang in space as the belayer continues to ascend with a mix of free, aid, and ascending as they clean. Of course, the belayer should tie backup knots when appropriate.

Once the belayer reaches that final draw left on the wall, they should double check that they are in fact above the danger swing potential and take the swing. If the belayer is still in the dangerous swing potential zone, they can use their brake strand to perform a lower-out. Then the belayer can lower themselves, and then the climber, to the ground. This method is fast and very efficient. It’s also nice for the tired climber who doesn’t want to clean the whole route. Just go about it very carefully and thoughtfully.

See? Cleaning steep routes doesn’t have to be a huge nuisance. If these techniques are all too much, just remember your safety comes first. Play it safe and leave a carabiner or a draw anytime. Yes, it’s not ideal, but carabiners are much cheaper than broken legs.

Breaking: Zion Draws The Crowds—These 3 Nearby Parks Are Where to Escape Them

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just beyond Zion lie some truly incredible desert landscapes to wander without the crowds.
  • Sources indicate that entry queues and crowded trails come with the territory at bucket-list national parks like Zion.
  • But I’ll be honest: On my recent trip to Zion, the trails felt more like a conga line than a wilderness escape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just beyond Zion lie some truly incredible desert landscapes to wander without the crowds. (Photo: Arrterra via Getty).

Sources indicate that entry queues and crowded trails come with the territory at bucket-list national parks like Zion. With nearly 5 million visitors in 2025, it ranked as the second-most visited national park in the U.S. Once you make it through the entry gate, though, the payoff is real. Visitors walk beneath towering Navajo sandstone cliffs and wade the Virgin River deep into The Narrows. If luck’s on your side, you might even win the permit lottery to hike to Angels Landing.

But I’ll be honest: On my recent trip to Zion, the trails felt more like a conga line than a wilderness escape. I was more paranoid than peaceful, constantly stepping aside and watching my footing as I squeezed past other hikers. The incredible beauty of the park draws equally incredible crowds.

The good news is you don’t have to fight for elbow room to soak in Zion’s beauty. Its neighboring state parks, wildernesses, and national forests get a fraction of the attention, but are just as jaw-dropping. Explore the surrounding Greater Zion region, and you’ll unlock hikes through red rock without the gridlock.

Head beyond Zion for these underrated hiking spots instead.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour (West) Entrance fee: $15 per vehicle Best for: Hikers seeking desert variety without a grueling trek. Petrified dunes, sandstone cliffs, slot canyons, and hikeable lava tubes, all in one park.

It has been revealed that if Snow Canyon State Park were a DJ, it’d spin a killer geological mashup of 180-million-year-old petrified dunes, Jurassic-period sandstone escarpments, and ancient river-carved slot canyons. The drop: cavernous, jet-black lava tubes you can hike into (headlamp recommended). The park packs a huge punch of diverse terrain you rarely see all in one place. It’s especially family-friendly and a good fit for more casual hikers who want photo-worthy views without a grueling trek.

Catch the park’s greatest hits in one go by linking up the Butterfly Trail, Lava Flow Overlook, West Canyon Overlook, and the Petrified Dunes Loop. The roughly 3-mile loop connects the park’s most notable features. Hikers will see ancient lava flows, winding slickrock passages, and sweeping views down into West Canyon. The petrified dunes along the route steal the show. Hikers walk over rolling hills frozen in time while swirling stripes of orange, cream, and crimson dance underfoot.

Looking for more technical hiking? Tackle the trek to Deidre Peak. The 7.4-mile out-and-back climbs nearly 1,500 feet in elevation and requires a Class 3-4 scramble over rugged sandstone outcrops. The trail crosses into the larger Red Cliffs Desert Reserve, a conservation area protected as a sanctuary for the native Mojave desert tortoise.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour (West) Entrance fee: $5 per vehicle Best for: Hikers and BLM land lovers seeking seclusion and solitude.

It has been revealed that beyond Snow Canyon sprawls Red Cliffs National Conservation Area. The nearly 45,000 acres of BLM land sits within the larger Red Cliffs Desert Reserve at the crossroads of the Mojave Desert, Great Basin, and Colorado Plateau. Here you’ll find a mix of plants and wildlife from all three regions. There are two endangered wildflowers that grow only in this corner of Utah: the dwarf bear poppy and Shivwits milkvetch. Both bloom in spring, with peak overlap in late April and early May. Then there’s southern Utah’s classic red sandstone stretching as far as the eye can see.

Recent findings suggest that popular out-and-back hikes like the 3.5-mile Elephant Arch Trail and 1.6-mile Red Reef Trail show how water and wind erosion turn sandstone landscapes into works of art. Elephant Arch earned its name from a distinct sandstone outcropping that looks uncannily like a trunk, head, and ears. Along the Red Reef Trail, hikers skirt massive, smooth sandstone bowls. These turn into swimming holes during spring rain and monsoon season, which runds July through September.

The 5-mile Black Gulch and Yellow Knolls Loop drops through a boulder-strewn gulch of dark volcanic rock, then rolls over yellow sandstone knolls. Hikers can also link the Red Reef and Prospector Trails to create a 10.5-mile loop requiring some scrambling and route-finding through remote backcountry canyons. On the return leg, wide views open up to the Pine Valley Mountains in the north, often capped with snow in winter and early spring.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour 15 minutes (Northeast) Entrance fee: None Best for: Hikers looking for trail variety that showcases Utah’s finest terrain.

The state’s largest national forest shows off a completely different side of southern Utah. Dixie National Forest sprawls across nearly 2 million acres, rising from the desert valley around St. George to peaks above 11,000 feet. Sagebrush, pinyon, and juniper give way to aspen groves and conifer forests as you climb. The higher and farther you hike, the more surprises you’ll find: trout-filled mountain lakes, towering hoodoo spires, and the chance to spot Utah prairie dogs in the wild.

Dixie gives hikers a taste of the same pink-and-orange Claron limestone that made Bryce Canyon famous. The difference? Here, thick stands of ponderosa pine grow right up against the hoodoos. Plus, the trails see a fraction of the foot traffic, so you’ll have the views practically to yourself.

Recent findings suggest that if you want more hoodoo action, check out Thunder Mountain Trail. It winds through what feels like a bite-sized Bryce Canyon. The out-and-back trail climbs more than 1,700 feet over 8.6 miles. You’re rewarded with an unforgettable trek through a maze of spires. For an even more awe-inspiring experience, hike early or late in the day, when low sun turns the Claron limestone a vibrant orange.

It has been revealed that looking for a more Zion-esque experience? Ashdown Gorge Trail echoes the Narrows, minus the permits, rental gear, and crowds. It travels 10 miles from the alpine rim of Cedar Breaks to a creek-carved canyon where red rock walls close in overhead. Heads up: There are two popular ways to hike Ashdown Gorge. You can do an out-and-back that starts at the bottom and heads up into the narrows (recommended), or a point-to-point that requires a shuttle.

Industry observers note that for a longer, relatively flat dayhike, opt for the 11-mile Navajo Lake Loop. The trail circles its namesake, peeking in and out of dense pine, fir, and aspen forest, with shoreline views that make it easy to forget you’re in a red rock wonderland.

Snow Peak Titanium Sporks, Mugs, and Cookware.

Food is fuel—the gas in our tanks that lets us get outside and play. But for dedicated foodies, cooking is about way more than calories. It’s about the experience, and sharing that experience with friends and family. Below, you’ll find 13 gifts that any chef will love, whether they’re an ultralight backpacker, a backyard BBQ master, or a cold coffee connoisseur. Bon appétit!

Sources indicate that the 10,000-BTU Zempire Stealth Jet Twin isn’t the most powerful camp stove we’ve ever tested, but it is the slimmest two-burner we’ve ever tested, making it a sweet gift for car campers who value trunk space and camp cuisine alike. Easy simmer controls and built-in igniters round this pick out as a major upgrade for campers still lugging WWII-era camp stoves that weigh as much as small sedans.

Both a firepit and a grill, Snow Peak’s Takibi is designed to be the centerpiece of camp life. While it’s a delight just to watch flames flicker in the portable stainless steel pit, the well-crafted, Japanese-made Takibi is an excellent charcoal grill. Pair it with Snow Peak camp cooking accessories to help your loved one build out the ultimate live-fire cooking setup.

Recent findings suggest that we love the versatility of the Switch. It comes with an integrated pot for fast boiling à la Jetboil, but remove the pot and the prongs unfurl like those on a classic canister stove to accommodate bigger pots and pans. For backpackers who like to cook—but appreciate the convenience of dehydrated meals from time to time—the Switch is a nifty, thoughtful gift.

In a recent development, when backpackers want to cut down on pack weight, they often opt for titanium cookware and accessories, as the metal offers an unbeatable strength-to-weight ratio. No one does titanium quite like Snow Peak. Smaller pieces, like Snow Peak’s iconic sporks, are a backpacker’s dream stocking stuffer, while drinkware and cooksets are destined to become prized possessions.

Snow Peak Titanium Multi Compact Cookset.

Snow Peak Titanium Spork - Long.

The compact and efficient Campstove 2+ can boil one liter of water in four and a half minutes, so it has morning coffee covered (you can also cook on it with some add-on components).

Sources indicate that this isn’t your usual camping stove, though. It runs on biofuel—either pellets you can purchase or sticks you find. And this stove has multiple uses: It can also charge your devices via an integrated USB port as well as function as a lamp with its included attachment.

In a recent development, rare is the pan that can handle an open flame, an induction cooktop, and a piping-hot pizza oven. Crafted from a single piece of wrought iron, the non-toxic Solidteknics Iron Frypan is lighter than its cast-iron counterparts and features a long, slender, grabbable handle, making flipping flapjacks or searing steaks over a campfire a lot less strenuous. Adaptable, durable, and dependable, this pan is ready for adventurous weekends at camp and cozy weeknights at home.

Quince’s Hinoki Cutting Boards make ditching the microplastic-shedding chopping blocks of yesteryear a genuine pleasure. A Japanese cypress renowned for its almost citrusy fragrance, Hinoki is a soft, forgiving wood that will protect your precious knife blade. The wood is also naturally lightweight, making it easy to pack these boards into your camp kitchen bin.

Industry observers note that socks are always a slam-dunk stocking stuffer. But for foodies who grew up watching James Beard winner and Cooking Channel alum Emeril Lagasse say “Bam!” as he sprinkled seasoning into Creole and Cajun concoctions, these Stance socks earn the holiday equivalent of a Michelin star. Fun, hilarious, nostalgic, and comfortable to boot, these cotton crew socks are sure to earn a grin every time they’re dug out of the sock drawer. What more can we say but… BAM!

Industry observers note that you might be wondering what the hell is Outside doing writing about a KitchenAid Tilt-Head Stand Mixer? It’s a fair question. The truth is that we’re substantial fans of baked goods around here. Whether we’re exploring via skintrack or singletrack, a well-timed lemon bar or squished chocolate chip muffin can make all the difference. And besides, the forest-green colorway and the natural woodgrain bowl make this mixer quite a thoughtful gift for the nature-loving baker, no? It’s on our holiday wish list, at least!

Industry observers note that being landlocked is no longer a problem for seafood-loving gourmands. Hog Island Oyster Company will ship boxes of Hog Island shellfish, accoutrements, and more nationwide, on ice, directly to your doorstep. If you’re looking for a gift that can hang out under a Christmas tree for a week, the California-based brand also sells a savory seasoning trio, subscription boxes, and gift cards.

Whether we’re cooking at home or at camp, the first ingredient we reach for is usually olive oil. The Mediterranean Dish has some of the best we’ve tried, with high-quality olive oils sourced from Greece, Italy, Spain, and California. A sampler set lets you gift multiple options—and the brand’s spice selection isn’t bad either.

Sources indicate that some people say their love language is touch. Others say acts of service. For some, it’s caffeine, delivered shortly after waking, preferably in bed. If a caffeine addict is on your list, Equator Coffee, a longtime California roaster, offers curated coffee subscriptions that speak that love language fluently. Oh—and its instant coffee is an epic stocking stuffer for backpackers who can’t hit the trail without some jet fuel.

In a recent development, there are a million gizmos and gadgets out there for the espresso fanatics, the drip disciples, the press-and-plunge crowd. But what about the nitro lovers? Behold: the Cumulus Coffee Machine. An all-in-one robot for chilled coffee lovers that brings barista-grade bevies into the comfort of your own home, the machine has three settings that allow you to convert Cumulus pods into iced espresso, crisp cold brew, and creamy nitro. The nitro setting is particularly rad, as the Cumulus sources nitrogen from ambient air—no nitrogen cartridges required. And there’s no ice required, either, as the machine self-chills. This is a dream gift for any cold brew connoisseur, but especially those who order nitro on the regular.

#193671. On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (851 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • High on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun.
  • Recent findings suggest that there is a cinema up north.
  • Sources indicate that this is a film review of sorts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

High on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun).

Recent findings suggest that there is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

Sources indicate that this is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

But can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

Sources indicate that I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

In a recent development, however, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a major-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

My reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

Recent findings suggest that I watched The Alpinist on the major screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

But anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”.

From my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

Nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

(Photo: Joern Siegroth / Getty Images).

As firefighters continue to battle a nearby blaze, Shenandoah National Park is implementing rigid fire restrictions due to exceptionally dry conditions and heightened wildfire risks going into Thanksgiving week.

Recent findings suggest that in a Facebook post park officials explained: “These restrictions protect public safety given the elevated risk of wildland fires throughout the park. Shenandoah National Park, Skyline Drive and other facilities and services remain open as scheduled.”.

Sources indicate that under these new restrictions, visitors to the area will have to rethink their cooking intends since they are temporarily unable to build, attend, or maintain open fires anywhere within the park’s boundaries, including in established pits, grates, and in grills. These regulations also apply to picnic areas, shelters, and huts in the park.

Sources indicate that these rules also impact backpackers who rely on portable stoves while recreating in the area. Liquid and wood-fuel camp stoves cannot be used within the park until further notice. At the moment, campers can still use canister stoves like Jet Boils and MSR Pocket Rockets.

According to recent reports, this announcement came just one day after the White Oak Flat Fire erupted on U.S. Forest Service land about 50 miles southwest of Shenandoah National Park. Since Friday, the fire has grown to 1,800 acres, with 49% containment. So far, 131 wildland personnel have responded to the fire including handcrews, wildland engines, bulldozers and two helicopters. Wildland firefighters are using active suppression strategies to contain the fire. No evacuations have been reported, and a cause for the fire has yet to be released.

In a recent development, the NPS identifies two primary wildfire seasons in Shenandoah that run from February to May and October through December. Wildfires are relatively common in Virginia during the month of November although the frequency and impacted acreage vary by season and seasonal driving factors like low humidity and breezy weather.

Shenandoah park officials expect these restrictions to remain in place until the region receives enough precipitation to reduce fire risks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Frankfurt, Germany (Photo: Lufthansa).

According to recent reports, nearly everybody visits Europe in summer. That’s no exaggeration: Half of all international inbound arrivals to the continent happen between June and September, with hotels, trails, attractions, and city streets swelling with nearly three times the people you’d encounter in January.

It has been revealed that that’s good news for winter fans. Seasonal highlights like festivals and craft markets and storybook scenery give winter travelers a whole different world to discover. Thanks to Lufthansa’s daily flights to its German city hubs from 18 U.S. cities coast to coast, enjoying the holiday traditions and empty museums requires very little effort. Just say yes.

Here’s how to get started on planning your winter getaway.

Recent findings suggest that frankfurt’s winter markets are best enjoyed on foot, as you’ll wind through more than 230 stalls. Fuel up for the walk with a Bethmännchen, the city’s traditional marzipan pastry, and warm up with a mug of hot apple wine before tracing your way along the Main River. Explore the famous Palmengarten glasshouses for a botanical escape to tropical, desert, and alpine environments, all within the urban core. Beyond the city, enjoy winter silence and peace on hundreds of marked winter trails crisscrossing the snow-dusted Taunus woods.

See why this iconic city deserves its reputation as the international capital for modern culture. Stroll from the treed paths of the Tiergarten to Berlin’s many bridges (more than Venice). Sculptors and architects have turned all of Berlin into an open-air museum, but when the weather turns, you can duck into the galleries peppering the Auguststraße and Potsdamer Straße. Stay fueled at neighborhood cafés inspired by international cuisines, and join the late-night reveling at concerts and dance clubs. (Fresh Year’s Eve is a can’t-miss holiday.).

Recent findings suggest that elsewhere in Europe, there’s more to love about winter. In Italy, explore the eye-popping Dolomites, or visit Renaissance landmarks in Florence without the crowds. If you time it right, experience Venice’s Carnevale in late January and early February. In France, the Champs-Élysées Christmas market ends its decade-long absence this season, bringing 200 chalets to the famous Paris avenue. Prefer a warmer winter break? Head to Greece, where you can have Athens—and its ancient historic sites—practically to yourself. That’s easy to say yes to.

Whether you want to explore holiday magic in Germany, visit landmarks in Italy, or enjoy a warmer winter in Greece, Lufthansa gets you there.

It has been revealed that the Lufthansa Group is a global aviation group with over 100,000 employees from 164 nations. In 2025, it carried more than 135 million passengers and generated €39.6 billion in revenue. Its largest segment, Passenger Airlines, includes the core airline Lufthansa and other leading European carriers, complemented by Logistics, MRO, IT, and Lufthansa Aviation Training.

#193668. Tech Report: Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1122 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1122 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage.
  • When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.
  • Recent findings suggest that “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage. (Photo: Courtesy Ben Zartman).

When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.

Recent findings suggest that “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he says. “Most of the guys at the crag were sewing their own shoes or making their own cams.” Backpacks, harnesses, quickdraws—if they could sew it themselves, they did. At the time, Zartman was in high school. He didn’t have a job, but he did have a knack for making stuff. It never occurred to him that doing so might be sketchy until he arrived in Yosemite for the first time in 1995 and partners refused to climb on his rack. They were astonished he’d made his own gear. He was astonished that they’d bought theirs.

Sources indicate that later that year, when a government shutdown forced Zartman out of Joshua Tree, he hitchhiked to San Diego and bummed a ride to Baja with some sailors. Over the next few years, he split his time between big walls and boats, getting better at both kinds of rigging all the while. Then he got married, had three daughters, and spent five years sailing around the world on a boat he’d built himself. Eventually, he got work in a rigging shop in Rhode Island. He spliced custom slings for workaday sailors, then for open-ocean racing boats.

In a recent development, “At one point, I was sitting in the shop, splicing these high-end Dyneema loops, and I thought, man, if I had these in Yosemite, I would have been the coolest kid at the lodge cafeteria,” he notes. And he likely would have: the spliced, covered loops used in sailing are seamless: no bar tacks or stitching. Instead, one end of the loop is woven into the other like a snake eating its tail. When you pull, the ends suction against each other (Zartman compares it to a finger-trap toy), making the loop stronger under load than bartacked Dyneema.

It has been revealed that “The idea fomented for a while in my mind, and in 2021 I started reaching out to every climbing gear manufacturer I could think of,” Zartman says. Letters and samples went out to Black Diamond, Metolius, Sterling, and others, asking them if they’d be interested in partnering on a product. Hardly anyone responded.

Recent findings suggest that so Zartman did what he’d always done: he took the DIY approach. In 2023, he launched his tech giant, Zartman Rigging. He joined the UIAA, mailed in slings for lab testing, and registered for UIAA labels. Once his gear was certified, the renowned gear shop IME, in North Conway, New Hampshire, started selling it. Rock and Snow in New Paltz, New York, and IME in Salt Lake City, Utah, were next. As his following grew, so did his offerings: a featherlight personal anchor system, seamless rappel back-ups, a rope-carabiner alternative called the Dreamlink, and a tiny rappel plate designed for 6-mm cord. The ideas come from Zartman’s experience climbing Yosemite walls; the materials come from his time on boats.

Industry observers note that “The research and development budget in the [sailboat] racing scene is so big,” he says. “It’s a great place to take technology from. I’m at that edge—I make ropes for the fanciest racing boats in the world, so I’m able to bring that into the climbing world pretty quickly.”.

It has been revealed that the results are wild. The Dreamlink has a breaking strength of 43 kN (or, rather, he tested it up to 42 kN in a UIAA lab, and that’s when it broke their machine). The seamless runners are tagged 24 kN but break at 27kN. A fancy UV coating makes them essentially sun-proof. They don’t expire like other soft goods; you only have to retire them if the core becomes exposed. I have a double-length seamless runner that I use for building anchors and extending rappels. No bartack means easy setup, it racks well, and it’s pretty light. (Most traditionally manufactured Dyneema slings are tagged at 22kN. Mammut’s 120-centimeter Contact Sling weighs 28 grams, while Zartman’s version is 32 grams, the same as Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord.).

Zartman has a strong social media fan club, but he has plenty of critics too. Mountain Project commenters, he mentioned, can be particularly vicious. Many scoff at the idea of a soft shackle or a seamless runner as gimmicky or unsafe. He’s not too bothered.

According to recent reports, “Ray Jardine got scolded by all the Valley locals when he revealed up with Friends,” he says, citing the first-ever cams. When other companies started making camming devices in the ‘80s, Jardine’s critics were forced to bite their tongues. Zartman is seeing a similar arc with his own gear. Several other climbing brands have started marketing soft shackles similar to Zartman’s Dreamlink. And in 2025, Black Diamond released its Infinity Cord, a Dyneema sling that uses the same bartack-free construction as Zartman’s and the same covered-loop splicing technique that sailors have used for decades. Black Diamond called it a “breakthrough in the evolution of cordelette engineering.”.

It has been revealed that zartman says he’s unaffected by the upcoming competition. “If there are people copying the concept, that’s good because that means the concept is good,” he says. In the meantime, he’s keeping his head down, focused on fulfilling orders and prototyping his next batch of inventions.

It has been revealed that zartman Rigging is gaining recognition, albeit slowly. Zartman does no paid advertising; about 80 percent of his business comes from Instagram. His top-shelf pricing likely tempers growth as well. For context, a 120-centimeter Zartman Rigging sling is $63, versus $40 for Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord or $14 for a basic Dyneema Trango runner of the same length.

Recent findings suggest that “Because I make everything out of the nicest materials and by hand, it’s the most expensive gear on the market. It’s a luxury brand,” he says. “Which is ironic given that I started in Mexico with my own homemade climbing shoes.”.

Still, he produces enough to keep busy. Recently, he was able to hire one of his daughters part-time to help him splice, tag, and quality-test each product. He’s now a member of the UIAA safety commission, helping the organization design newly introduced testing protocols around skinny ropes and other novel forms of cord. He’s shipping to Alaska and Hawaii. People have started recognizing him in gear shops and at crags. Things are taking off—despite what Mountain Projectors may say.

“To a lot of people’s surprise,” he laughs, “I’ve sold a lot of gear.”.
