This is your moment. You may be thinking: But I’m not going to be climbing much for the next few months. I’ll just wait.

It has been revealed that real ones know that would be a grave error. Come February or March, you will still need latest shoes. But chance are, they’ll be full price. Plus, if you initiative ahead and invest now, you can spend the winter breaking them in around the gym. Here are a few standout Black Friday climbing deals on rock and approach shoes to consider below.

Industry observers note that if your footwork repertoire involves pockets and micro edging, the La Sportiva Miura VS Climbing Shoe is among the best. Last year, we chose the Miura VS as the best tech shoe out there. With an aggressive downturn and semi-stiff, low-profile toe box, this shoe is perfect for precision climbing up slab and narrow cracks. Note that VS means this shoe uses a Velcro closure.

It has been revealed that la Sportiva’s Katana is an awesome technical shoe for edging and beyond. Note that the men’s version is stiffer than the women’s version. This shoe is great for precision placements on slab, narrow cracks, and steep routes. After a buddy gifted me his slightly too small Katanas, I had them resoled and have been loving them indoors and out. You can also check out our review of the Katana here.

Recent findings suggest that with great grip and breathability, these approach shoes strike a near-perfect balance between nimble hiking and climbing performance—without the weight. That’s why we selected the TX2 Evo as our top pick for a lightweight approach shoe last year. We also love that La Sportiva crafts this pair with recycled materials and a sole designed for easy repairs. This is one of the best Black Friday climbing deals out there if you need a good approach shoe.

We haven’t seen deals this pervasive on shoes in a while. All but ONE of the dozen pairs we gave top billing in our Fall 2026 Shoe Guide are marked down right now at Backcountry. (The only shoe that evaded discounts is the Scarpa Furia Air, our top pick for a “soft/high-feedback” shoe.) You can read our testers’ thoughts on each shoe in our guide, and see the deals on each shoe and what it’s best for below.

The Red Chili Voltage: “a sleeper classic—a tautly crafted, downturned, asymmetrical performance sport shoe with a solid crossover into bouldering.”.

Scarpa VSR LV: “Across a range of styles and grades, testers praised the shoe’s precision on tiny footholds and its power on steep terrain.”.

La Sportiva Ondra Comp: “Maybe the best toe-hooking shoe I have encountered—ever.”.

Mad Rock D2 One: “… I can safely call these the most versatile, ideal for both bouldering and sport.”.

Butora Ibex: “Hardcore boarders, boulderers, and comp climbers will love it, though I also found it versatile for vertical edging.”.

Evolv Phantom Pro: “… offers significant-time driving and grabbing power paired with a velvety, forgiving footbed and single-strap, sock-like closure.”.

Ocún Jett S: “For a ‘narrow’ slipper, the Jett S still has enough lateral stretch to accommodate wide feet, with a comfy last great for long gym sessions—both bouldering and sport.”.

La Sportiva Mantra: “With a major downcamber and mild asymmetry, the sensitive and pared-down Mantra is great for grabbing big, smeary holds.”.

Evolv Zenist Pro: “The Zenist Pro stands out for its edging and all-around prowess, and is perhaps not as smeary or grabby as the marketing would have you believe.”.

Scarpa Generator Mid: ““The Generator Mid’s major toe box was adept at rand smearing in a sustained corner crack and for the wide stuff, but boxy and insensitive in thin jams.”.

Update: This shoe has sold out at Backcountry since we first published this deals round-up.

Scarpa Blackbird: “Over months of testing, the Blackbird has certainly lived up to its hype and its price … The edging power on the Blackbird is off the charts, with the best support and stability on square-cut edges of any shoe I’ve worn.”.

It has been revealed that beyond shoes, there’s a lot more climbing gear on sale out there during Black Friday. Ropes, hardware, and more are all marked down 20% or more. Here are our top editor-tested picks.

It has been revealed that most climbers care about the planet. We can do our part in a lot of ways, one of which is buying more planet-friendly gear. Edelrid manufactured this 70m rope with over 40% renewable materials, leveraging a bio-based polyamide in part made from castor oil. This is the first synthetic rope of its kind that relies less heavily on fossil fuels. Of course, the rope has to work, too, and in tests, we found it held up well. It feeds well and proved kink-resistant in our tests. We dubbed it the best eco-friendly cord in our 2025 rope guide.

Recent findings suggest that we tested Mammut’s Alpine Core Protect Rope and called it one of the safest ropes we’d ever used. It also held up remarkably well after significant abuse in the field. By weaving burly aramid fibers into its core, this innovative rope from Mammut helps resist cutting. And right now, you can snag it at 20% off.

It has been revealed that using the same cam-assisted blocking that makes the Grigri the safer choice over an ATC or other devices, the NEOX innovates with an integrated wheel that makes feeding out slack when lead belaying faster and smoother. Petzl also engineered the NEOX with recycled materials to reduce its environmental impact. We’ve used it for rock, gym, and ice climbing and we’re big fans.

According to recent reports, I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air. The pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack.

A chance to save on cams? We’ll take it. Snag one (or a few) of this Black Diamond #.5 to enhance your rack for fast and light missions.

Our top all-around harness of Fall 2026, the Solution uses what Black Diamond dubs Contour Edge Technology for the waist and leg loops, meaning they’re more rigid in the middle, but flexible and soft at the edges for increased comfort. One of our testers found that this made for a climbing harness with “fantastic” hip support. It didn’t cause any uncomfortable pressure or distracting pain points on his body, steadfastly supporting him during 10-hour days on the wall.

One of our editors’ favorite gifts for this holiday season, Trango’s REAL Chalk is better for humans and the planet. This seawater-sourced chalk comes in 50g, 250g, or 500g bags. Makes for a great stocking stuffer—or stock up for yourself for 2027.

I bought a BD Momentum Full-Body Harness in 2018 or 2019 and am still using it today. It’s been through years of indoor and outdoor climbing with both of my kids. It’s user-friendly, too—a four-year-old can handle putting it on themselves. When my son finally outgrows his next spring, it’s in good enough shape that we will pass it down to another climbing family. This is a great time to save on a kids’ harness that will last until your kid outgrows it.

Perhaps the most hyped carabiner of 2026 (if there is such a thing as carabiner hype), the Magnetron returned by popular demand a few months ago. After promptly going out of stock, what’s been billed as “Alex Honnold’s favorite carabiner” is now back in inventory—and on sale. The biggest boon of this cult-favorite gear is that you can never forget to lock it, thanks to an automatic magnetic locking mechanism. However, it’s not great for ice/alpine climbing and can be a tad difficult to operate for smaller hand sizes. I personally have a small hand and find it easy to use and love it. But you can read our full thoughts here.

One of our top ice tool picks this winter, the Black Diamond Hydras offer an impeccably balanced swing, ultra-precise pick, and a high degree of modularity make the Black Diamond Hydra our tool of choice for moderate and vertical ice. Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. Read more about the Hydras in our Winter Gear Guide.

Our best all-around helmet of Fall 2026, the Black Diamond Vision offers the best of both worlds when it comes to comfort and weight. Made from mostly foam, with a plastic, ABS hardshell covering a portion of the top of the helmet, the Vision is impressively light at 215 grams.

After rapidly burning through Black Diamond Crack Gloves (that broke within a few months while climbing an indoor crack), I ordered a pair of these Ocún gloves a couple years ago and have loved them ever since. They are easy to put on, simple to clip to a back gear loop of your harness (I keep them clipped under my chalkbag), comfortable, and super durable on sandstone, granite, and human-made cracks alike.

It has been revealed that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

It has been revealed that overlanding is a pretty niche activity, so it can be hard to find the perfect gift for the driver in your life. Fear not. As an overlander myself, I’ve compiled a comprehensive gift list that has suggestions for overland rookies and veterans alike. I’ve included a wide range of price options, with some gift ideas so big they’ll take up half your living room and others small enough to fit under the tree.

Tires are the most important overland upgrade. A good set of all-terrain tires like the BFGoodrich KO3s helps drivers safely get through snow and mud, and up and down rocky backcountry roads. Their tougher construction also helps resist flats. I love the KO3s for their legendary off-road reliability combined with their quiet ride on pavement.

Overlanders love to get stuck so they can get back out, which makes recovery gear essential. Maxtrax boards slip under tires that have lost traction, allowing the vehicle to slowly inch out of snow, mud, sand, or whatever else it’s bogged down in. Go for the more expensive Xtreme version because it comes with metal traction teeth that last significantly longer.

Sources indicate that airing down tires is often the easiest way to get unstuck because it increases the tires’ contact patch. I love the Rhino kit because it airs down four tires at once. I also recommend this ARB air compressor that attaches to a car battery and can reinflate the tires before you hit pavement again.

Sources indicate that sometimes self-recovery isn’t an option after getting stuck, and I’ve had to get yanked out by a friend. This device fits in the two-inch rear receiver on any truck or SUV and creates a safe place to attach a D-ring and recovery strap. Heads up: Make sure whoever you gift this to knows how to use it properly before heading out.

Sources indicate that folded down, this shovel is only 18 inches long. Fully extended, it goes to 34 inches and is perfect for digging your truck out of a snowbank or excavating a cathole near camp. I’ve tested an earlier version of this shovel for years, and the carbon steel head has put up with rocks, trees, and firm ground without ever bending or chipping.

Sources indicate that anyone who’s overlanding for more than a couple of days will love an electric fridge. It eliminates ice runs and keeps food from drowning in meltwater. Dometic makes some of the most reliable fridges on the market. I like this one because it has two zones: one a fridge, the other either a fridge or a freezer.

Coffee tastes better at 9,000 feet. To brew it there, Yeti’s indestructible French press is my go-to. I’ve thrown it in a kitchen box or just let it roll around in the back of my truck, and it still works perfectly every time. I also love that it has a ceramic lining so the coffee doesn’t taste like metal.

Water can be a precious commodity on a backcountry trip. That’s why I use this battery-powered faucet that pulls water from a jug and then dispenses just the right amount so I can wash my hands or do dishes. One charge lasts for weeks, and all the hoses are easy to clean at home. Pair it with a Dometic water jug for the ideal setup.

The REDARC GoBlock is my go-to overland battery (for fridges, lights, etc.) because it’s designed to be charged in multiple ways. I can connect solar panels to add juice at camp, or I can wire it to my alternator so it gets topped off while I’m driving. I recommend the kit version, which includes a dock that bolts to a truck bed and gives the battery a secure place to live at all times.

Sources indicate that iKamper nailed the details with this version of the Skycamp rooftop tent. It has the smartest mounting system I’ve tested. The bombproof hardshell cover will put up with years of sun and weather, and inside it’s extra roomy thanks to a clever tent design. It’s pricey, but this is one of those buy-once, cry-once purchases that you’ll have for at least a decade.

Two layers of enhanced memory foam make the Foamy the most comfortable camping mat on the market. Nothing else I’ve tested even comes close. Perfect for larger tents or truck beds, the Foamy almost guarantees a good night’s sleep because it’s so plush. Pair it with a camping blanket and the setup will be almost as comfortable as what you’re used to at home.

In a recent development, overlanding requires a lot of gear. The best way to keep it all organized is a Kitworks Gear Box. Infinitely customizable, the Gear Box is the perfect storage method for a camp kitchen, recovery gear, dry food, even clothing. Made from honeycomb panels covered in a 900-denier ripstop shell, the box has proven just as durable as any hard-sided competitor.

Sources indicate that don’t invest in a dash-mounted radio—get two of these instead. With an ultra-reliable, multi-day battery and huge range, these radios are the best way to stay in touch with buddies when cell phones don’t work. When I’m not using the radios in my truck, I use them to keep in contact while backcountry skiing, hunting, and other off-grid adventures.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Since the dawn of time, the base layer/midlayer/shell sandwich has been the go-to for winter adventures. But for runners, a good jacket paired with just a technical T-shirt or long-sleeve is often a better choice. Today’s jackets use the latest advances in insulation and waterproofing to replace two or three traditional layers, and adapt better to changing conditions and activity levels.

According to recent reports, the jackets in this review proved sufficiently lightweight, breathable, and weatherproof that we rarely had to remove them to manage heat—and when we did, it was much easier to deal with one item than several. We tested these jackets in conditions ranging from wind-blown fall rain to frigid cold mountain mornings, and they consistently kept us moving forward with minimal fuss, wrapped in warmth and shielded from the elements.

Pros and Cons + Surprisingly warm + Unrestrictive fit + Smart vent panels – No hood.

The Thermalrunner proved an excellent choice for a surprisingly broad range of temperatures and weather conditions. On a blustery 40-degree day with light rain, the water-resistant fabric treatment handled the challenge, beading moisture on the exterior while the soft interior lining stayed dry against the skin. On another run when the sun burned through clouds unexpectedly fast, we were impressed by how well the vent panels in the back shed excess heat. One tester called the lightweight PrimalLoft insulation a “Goldilocks” amount of warmth that consistently tamed the chill without overheating him.

This jacket features all the premium touches you’d want, including zip hand pockets and chest pouch, reflective patches, and a slightly extended, insulated back panel that added extra warmth and protection from the elements. Paired with a light, short-sleeved base layer, the Thermalrunner jacket was comfortable for running on mild 50-degree days, and with a hat (it lacks a hood), gloves, and a long-sleeve undergarment, it handled near-freezing weather just as well.

Pros and Cons + Featherweight + Packable + Protective hood – Fragile.

Stuffing the Aerolight Wind Jacket into a pack before heading out on an adventurous mountain trek in the Swiss Alps proved to be a good decision for one tester. Late in the afternoon, the summer skies filled with clouds, the temperature dropped, and bursts of rain started soaking the mountainside. The jacket provided immediate warmth, blocked the wind, and, though it’s by no means waterproof, kept enough moisture out to keep moving comfortably—with almost no weight penalty.

The water-resistant treatment is PFAS-free, and small touches like an adjustable hood and elastic wrist cuffs add to the better-than-expected protection. The ultralight fabric is soft and quiet on the move and breathes well at high exertion levels, but offers no stretch. The lone chest pocket doubles as a stuff sack, making this a great item to keep on hand for mild days in the 40s and 50s. The feather-weight construction comes at the price of being somewhat more fragile than other top picks: we’ve heard reports of the fabric blowing out under stress, although we didn’t see any excess wear during testing.

Pros and Cons + Windproof + Highly visible + Distinctive look – Lacks breathability.

Recent findings suggest that when was the last time someone on the street complimented your running outfit for looking good? Our testers got compliments on the PYNRS (pronounced like “pioners”) Magnolia Track Jacket all the time. This NYC-based company started as an inclusive urban running club before branching into apparel; the result is functional outerwear that stands out from the crowd.

The iridescent, tightly woven nylon shell features reflective piping for excellent visibility from all sides, and the polyester lining is soft against skin. Cut on the looser side, this jacket easily accommodated insulating layers and proved comfortable for running in near- and sub-freezing weather. It offers roomy, zippered hand pockets and an interior zippered chest pocket, plus elasticized cuffs and a drawstring waist to seal out the weather. The jacket is a little hefty and lacks some of the breathability higher-performance materials offer, but for cool-to-cold weather running (low 40s to mid-20s), we stayed comfortably warm and looked stylish in the Magnolia Track Jacket.

Start ready and stay ready with this do-anything hooded workout layer. Crafted from a soft performance stretch knit, this jacket is both insulating and flexible with a protective woven overlay that gives you added coverage in cool and variable conditions. It wicks moisture and includes a drawcord hood and zip pockets to keep you and your belongings dry and safe in any weather. Pair it with the Vuori Sunday bottoms to make the perfect set.

Pros and Cons + Soft wool fabric + Polartec insulation + Wind-blocking torso – No reflectivity.

The Alpha Active’s medium-weight blend of Merino wool and polyester, with a touch of bamboo rayon, proved exceptionally soft and warm, and excelled at wicking moisture away from skin. Baffled Polartec Alpha insulation and a wind-blocking nylon fabric overlay the chest. The overall effect felt like wearing a lightweight vest over a premium base-layer shirt—but integrated into a single piece that moved comfortably and quietly with us.

The breathable Merino-blend sleeves and back, with no wind-blocking material, kept us from overheating at easier paces up to the 50-degree mark. The jacket proved comfortable down to freezing when working hard—adding a lightweight outer shell produced a warm combination that handled all but the most bitter or windy conditions. The sleek fit and black fabric look good, but bring a reflective hat or wear a light for nighttime running.

Pros and Cons + Toasty, 95% recycled fleece front + Functional and stylish fit + Solid warmth – No backside windblock.

Sources indicate that our testers agreed that the front of this attractive jacket provided solid insulation for frigid conditions. They were divided, however, on whether it would have benefited from better wind-blocking on the back, where a large fabric panel vented heat, leaving some feeling too exposed to the elements. Still, at an affordable price, most reviewers found the Winter Warm Pro kept them comfortable in temperatures well below freezing (there’s no hood, so bring a hat for frigid days). The body fabric fleece is made with 95 percent recycled materials, feels soft against bare skin, and stretches nicely. The polyester torso insulation is reassuringly thick without feeling bulky. Additional touches include a water-repellent coating, hand pockets, side mesh storage pocket, and a zippered chest pocket.

Pros and Cons + Stormproof + Effective hood and brim + Chest snap – Crinkly.

Salomon’s adv.DRY material—a thin, microporous membrane bonded to a nylon shell—proved impressively waterproof during drenching rain showers while staying breathable in dry conditions. The Bonatti Pro features fully taped seams, waterproof zippers, and an excellent, adjustable brimmed hood that kept our hair dry and our heads warm without impeding our field of vision, even on the move. A snap closure at the chest lets you open the zipper and vent heat rapidly without removing the jacket, and reflective patches on the front and back provide good visibility in poor weather.

Sources indicate that the fit is close yet roomy enough to accommodate insulating underlayers, extending the jacket’s comfortable range below the freezing mark. The fabric is somewhat crinkly, but it still packs easily into a small bundle. There are vents at the waist, but they’re fairly minimal, and we didn’t notice much airflow. Salomon’s “aeroPACK” flap system is meant to accommodate a small hydration backpack without impeding the jacket’s fit; we didn’t test this feature but noted that it didn’t get in the way when running without a pack.

Choosing the best winter running jacket is primarily about the kinds of winter conditions you face where you live, travel, and run. Consider if you need a waterproof layer, or can get by with water resistance—waterproof jackets are more costly, don’t breathe as well, and tend to be somewhat stiffer and noisier, but are worth it when you’re out in a downpour or blizzard.

Sources indicate that then think about whether you want your running jacket to be insulated and provide warmth on its own, or work as a thin, exterior shell layer. Insulated jackets can make heading out in frigid temps less daunting, especially if you tend to run cold, but can get hot during high-intensity exercise or if the temps rise. Shell jackets allow you to layer underneath to adjust for a range of conditions. Also consider whether you want a fitted jacket that stays close to the body for streamlined mobility, or a looser fit that allows flexibility for layering underneath.

It has been revealed that the jacket review test crew put these products through their paces in locations as diverse as the Swiss Alps and Nebraska’s High Plains, logging miles on both roads and trails. Testers recorded their notes for each sample piece during easy runs, up-tempo workouts, and everything in between, in good weather and full-on storm conditions. Jackets were evaluated for their effectiveness at keeping testers warm and blocking wind and moisture while breathing and venting excess heat, with bonus points given for the versatility to handle a range of weather conditions and to look good in diverse contexts.

In a recent development, lead reviewer Mark Eller is based in Boulder, Colorado. He’s logged three Boston Marathons, completed trail-running ultras, and has raced in multiple off-road and on-road triathlons. He also enjoys snowboarding and Nordic skiing on Colorado’s Front Range and central mountains, and he frequently rows a single scull at the Boulder Reservoir.

Brian Metzler is a freelance writer and the founding editor of Trail Runner. A former walk-on Division I track athlete, he mostly runs on mountainous trails nowadays in Boulder and Leadville, Colorado.

Recent findings suggest that kurt Actenhagen enjoys trail running, mountain biking, and exploring mountain ranges from the High Sierra to Colorado’s most remote peaks. What Climbers Should Know About Intrusive Thoughts

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the author climbing in Big Cottonwood Canyon in northern Utah.
  • Warning: The following piece includes several examples of intrusive thoughts, including acts of violence in a climbing setting.
  • In a recent development, have you ever been 50 feet or so off the deck when an intrusive thought suddenly disrupts your climbing?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the author climbing in Big Cottonwood Canyon in northern Utah. Her most prevalent intrusive thought? The rope is going to cut. (Photo: Casey Coleman).

Warning: The following piece includes several examples of intrusive thoughts, including acts of violence in a climbing setting. It does not constitute treatment or medical advice, and is not intended for individuals with Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

In a recent development, have you ever been 50 feet or so off the deck when an intrusive thought suddenly disrupts your climbing? Maybe it’s about something you forgot to do—lock your doors, extinguish your campfire, or put your dog outside. For a lot of us, it’s fear-based: I’m going to deck and break my ankles. Sometimes, it’s more sinister: I should let go of the brake strand or I should untie my knot.

Intrusive thoughts are more common than you might think. A 2014 study across 13 countries found that 93.6% of university students reported experiencing intrusive thoughts at least once during the previous three months. Stress is known to be one of the most common triggers of intrusive thoughts. So in a sport with an entire cottage industry around psychologically outsmarting the fear response, could intrusive thoughts be even more likely to emerge?

Industry observers note that while no studies exist on intrusive thoughts among climbers, a new book touches upon these unwanted notions that sometimes prey upon our minds. In Get a Grip, psychotherapist-climber Joel Robertson, MA MBACP, and coach Louis Parkinson guide climbers toward adopting a healthier mindset. They tackle constructively reframing comparisons to other climbers and setting realistic goals. Ultimately, they show climbers that we are not the equivalent of our thoughts—even the unwelcome, unpleasant, or truly intrusive ones.

“We are not our thoughts, and our thoughts are not objective truth,” Robertson states.

After giving Get a Grip a read, we asked our readers to tell us about some of the strangest intrusive thoughts they’ve experienced in climbing on Instagram. From the innocuous (Did that fart come with a price?) to the dark (What if my belayer dies and I fall?), 119 climbers responded with fears they’ve had to ignore on the wall.

A few climbers shared intrusive thoughts about their belayer. What if they stopped paying attention—or passed out? Or more disturbingly: “What if my boyfriend decides he wants to murder me right now and just lets me fall?” (Sadly, that’s not totally unfounded.) Only one belayer shared an urge-based intrusive thought about taking their climber off belay—and jumping off the wall.

Perhaps that climber experienced what’s known in French as “l’appel du vide,” or “the call of the void.” One researcher describes this phenomenon as “fleeting, involuntary urges to engage in dangerous actions, most often in situations involving heights or other perceived risks.”.

Most of the intrusive thoughts centered, unsurprisingly, on gear failure and falling. Did I forget to tie in properly? What if the rope cuts (my personal recurring intrusive thought)? And what does a factor 2 fall feel like?

Some expressed anxieties about wildlife on the wall. A few climbers worried about spiders and bees lurking in cracks. They envisioned mountain goats knocking them off the route and rattlesnakes looming on ledges.

Others shared intrusive urges: Skip every clip, remove your Grigri, just jump. Only one climber mentioned they didn’t have any such thoughts: “Climbing is the one thing that quiets the intrusive thoughts with any sort of reliability.”.

With all of these ruminations externalized, I wondered whether we might be more likely to have intrusive thoughts while engaged in the sometimes high-stress activity of climbing. “I would say the process of climbing is one that may be affected by intrusive thoughts more than others,” Robertson says. Beyond prevalence, coping with these thoughts on a high-stakes climb can present more of a challenge. You can’t always fully stop what you’re doing to refocus your mind.

“While climbing, I think intrusive thoughts may be more noticeable, feel more difficult to manage, and pose more potential risk to physical safety, as compared with other pursuits that are less intensive, require less focus, and/or have us in situations of less physical risk,” Robertson notes.

So for the climbers who battle these internal distractions, what should we do when unwanted ruminations enter our minds?

In Get a Grip, Robertson and Parkinson outline a three-step process for dealing with all varieties of intrusive thoughts.

Industry observers note that most importantly, don’t panic at the thought you’re having. Frantically trying to eradicate it from your mind might backfire. The first step? Recognize what’s entered your mind. “Acknowledge the thought and listen to it,” Robertson recommends. ”Don’t try and banish the thought.”.

It has been revealed that sometimes, you might be having the thought for a reason. After all, anxiety about whether you tied in harks back to a long-time complacency trap in climbing: Forgetting to properly tie your knot.

Recent findings suggest that “Listen to the thought and see if it’s got any wisdom,” Robertson advises. For example, check your tie-in knot, if that’s what you’re worried about. Call down to your belayer and ask them to watch you. Or evaluate that last cam—and re-place it more securely or add a second piece—if ripping gear is what’s haunting your mind.

If you’re having an intrusive thought about something you can’t do anything about right now—like whether you forgot to turn off the oven at home—the goal is to manage the thought until you can do something about it, like texting your roommate to check the stove or until you can finish the route and get home.

Then tell the thought, “I’ve heard you and I’ve acknowledged you. I’m putting you to the side.”.

Next, move forward. “Decide on a thing that you are going to think about now instead,” Robertson explains.

Sources indicate that most importantly, redirect your focus to something specific. So it’s not, “Now I’m going to focus on climbing this route,” or “Okay, time to think about something else.” Rather, it’s, “I’m going to imagine exactly how that crimp up there feels on my right fingers,” then put your hand on it. Robertson indicates it’s about “deliberately choosing to focus on things that aren’t the unhelpful intrusive thought.”.

An important thing to remember and accept is that your intrusive thought is probably not just going to disappear altogether. “It’s going to come back, but that’s fine,” Robertson explains. “Just know that it’s a process.” Try not to fret about or dread the prospect of the thought returning. Just keep acknowledging, refocusing, and moving up the wall.

What if you’re having an intrusive thought as a belayer versus as the climber? Robertson indicates to apply the same logic. But if it’s truly a distracting thought, it might be best to ask your climber to get to a safe stance (e.g., clip and take, or gain a ledge) while you regain your full concentration on belaying. Pause, do some breathing work, acknowledge, and redirect, Robertson advises.

According to recent reports, since stress can lead to intrusive thoughts, and climbing can be stressful, Get a Grip highlights the importance of distinguishing between the good kind of stress and the bad kind of stress. Trad climber Hazel Findlay reflects on this in the book as well.

Recent findings suggest that with distress, you feel out of control—and you’re not having any fun. Maybe you started up a route that is too far outside your limit. Or perhaps conditions are taking a turn for the worse and you’re trying to push through anyway. If you’re distressed, it might be best to back off, change course, or reconsider your approach if possible.

In a recent development, in the case of eustress, Robertson says you might feel some fear and not calm, but it’s more of a butterflies-in-your-stomach vibe, than a panicked “What have I gotten myself into?” situation. “It feels fun; it feels exciting,” Robertson says.

In a recent development, to seek eustress and avoid distress, Parkinson recommends making accurate risk assessments based on your past experiences before committing to a climb. Think back through all of the precautions you’re taken—partner checks, researching the route, trusting your belayer. Then conjure up past analogous experiences of eustress that you powered through. “I recommend thinking back on similar situations with similar levels of fear that you’ve survived successfully,” Parkinson notes. “I do that for myself when I get scared on something.”.

Parkinson will acknowledge the fear or intrusive thought, then talk himself through it: “This feels scary, but it feels scary in a really similar way to something I’ve done before. And I managed to do that, so I’m going to carry on with this level of fear for a bit longer if I can.”.

#193643. She Asked the Appalachian Trail Conservancy to Start an Artist Residency. Now You Can Apply, Too.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (892 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

She Asked the Appalachian Trail Conservancy to Start an Artist Residency. Now You Can Apply, Too.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Philadelphia metalsmith Mallory “Bullseye” Weston wanted to apply for an artist residency on the Appalachian Trail, she ran into a problem.
  • It has been revealed that so she sent a cold email.
  • It has been revealed that from her Philadelphia studio, Weston had a sense of what a good walk could yield.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Philadelphia metalsmith Mallory “Bullseye” Weston wanted to apply for an artist residency on the Appalachian Trail, she ran into a problem. They didn’t have one.

It has been revealed that so she sent a cold email. Within a few hours, Dakota Jackson, senior director of visitor engagement at the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC) had written back to set up a meeting. It was perfect timing: The ATC was approaching its centennial in 2025 and looking for newly introduced ways to get more hikers on trail. As Caroline Ralston, the ATC’s associate vice president of marketing and communications, put it, “at that time, we realized we didn’t really have anything for creatives.”.

It has been revealed that from her Philadelphia studio, Weston had a sense of what a good walk could yield. She’d already put in miles on the John Muir Trail (JMT), the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), and the Tahoe Rim Trail, and was starting to see a clearer connection between her creative life and her hiking.

Recent findings suggest that A 454-mile stretch of the PCT found its way into 30 titanium brooches shaped like lengths of paracord. Their colors and patterns changed with her mood on the trail, day by day. Her stories became a zine. So when she and Jackson started talking through possible structures for the ATC’s inaugural artist in residence program, she offered herself up as the guinea pig.

In a recent development, last year, when the Conservancy officially rolled out the program, Weston set out from Georgia as its pilot creative. “Almost a year after I planted the seed for this wild idea, somehow, things came together to make it a reality,” Weston wrote in her blog.

Since metalwork is specialized and far from portable, she used the hike as an inspiration gathering exercise rather than a time to actually create work. She couldn’t haul a forge, but she could carry a camera. Back in Philadelphia, she’s been picking through her thousands of photographs, taking another look at the pile of butterfly wings she came across, or the blazes she passed.

“Hiking the trail as the ATC’s Artist in Residence has motivated me to be more observant of my surroundings,” Weston told the ATC. “I’ve been actively documenting the experience through photography and journaling, wanting to remember the rich details of my hike and use them to generate artwork from the vivid text and images I’ve collected.”.

Weston had one piece finished before she ever set foot on the AT. For the trail’s centennial, she designed an enamel pin that hikers could pick up at a visitor center.

Sources indicate that the ATC is now looking for its 2027 Artist in Residence, and artists working in any medium have until January 3, 2027, to apply. The residency includes a limited stipend for transportation and lodging for events along the AT, and a two- to four-week stay at Maine’s Monson Arts, an arts center in the last town NOBO hikers pass through before the 100-Mile wilderness. Weston spent five months walking the entire AT, but the next resident could hike a section or spend their time in one town along the trail; the residency’s structure is malleable.

“This program is a new way to experience the trail,” says Ralston. “When the trail was first conceptualized over 100 years ago, one of the founding ideas was that people need a place to escape, connect with nature, and unplug. This program is an extension of that. We want to invite artists to immerse themselves on the trail, connect with nature, and see what kind of inspiration comes from it.”.

Sources indicate that along with a résumé or CV and five to 10 work samples, applicants must provide an artist statement and a work proposal. The ATC wants to know what you make, what time on the trail might bring to your work, and how you’d share it.

What makes an application stand out? For Ralston, notable applications will express “a desire to get out there, and a desire to share it publicly.” For Weston, that meant giving talks at trail centers.

It has been revealed that her advice to the next applicant? Think about what a stretch of time on this particular trail might change about the work you already do, and leave yourself some room to be surprised. For Weston, one of those surprises came in her first week out of Georgia.

Recent findings suggest that the first time Weston spotted pink lady’s slipper orchids on the AT, her husband was hiking with her. He’d come along for the first stretch and they saw a few patches together that week. Each flower had a little pouch that she found “kind of weird and grotesque looking, but also very beautiful.” By the time she came across a whole field of them, her husband had gone home to Philadelphia. “I’m all alone, and here’s all these orchids,” she remembers thinking.

According to recent reports, now, back in her Philadelphia studio, she’s working on a recreation of a pink lady’s slipper. Of all the things she saw in five months on trail, that one made what she calls a “one to one translation” into her work.

“Now that I’m back in Philadelphia, I’m distilling all of that experience into work that emerges from it,” says Weston.

Industry News: The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting Latest Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Key Than Ever.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1723 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc.
  • The trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees.
  • Industry observers note that moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc. (Photo: Getty).

The trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees. After hearing the now-familiar heavy breaths of runners behind me, I move to the mountainside to let them pass. It’s mid-August, and the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB), the ultramarathon circling Mont Blanc, is kicking off later this month in Chamonix. We started our own Tour du Mont Blanc in Chamonix, the mountain town known as the birthplace of alpinism, which was buzzing with excitement and packs of runners strapped into hydration packs. Ahead of me, a young man is stopped on the narrow dirt trail, calling out to a friend on the forest slope below. Before I can even turn around, our guide, Jason Day, springs into action, grabs a rope from his pack, and helps pull the hiker, whose pack had tumbled down the slope, back to safety.

Industry observers note that moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland. Roughly 80,000 people hike it each year, and visits are up about 50 percent since 2020. “People can only see the backsides of those in front of them,” Jean-Marc Peillex, mayor of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, a mountain town at the base of Mont Blanc in France, told Swiss broadcaster SRF. That wasn’t my exact experience for most of the trek, but in a few places, especially near Chamonix, the trail was congested.

It has been revealed that chamonix and the six other French towns along the TMB route, from Vallorcine to Bourg-Saint-Maurice and Beaufort, have drafted a charter to manage crowds, with local officials aiming to put it in place by spring 2027, ahead of next year’s trekking season. The new rules, aiming to curb overtourism and help slow environmental damage, are awaiting final signature. The key proposals include reservations for every night on the trail; a ban on wild camping, with paid, bookable bivouac areas replacing the informal spots; and new limits on luggage transfers. Guided groups would be capped at twelve and led by guides trained in rescue and licensed in all three countries.

According to recent reports, the charter is voluntary, covers only France for now, and still depends on local ordinances for enforcement. But the message is clear: the era of showing up and figuring it out on the TMB is ending. Chamonix’s mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, who is similarly introducing quotas at nearby Lac Blanc, an alpine lake also suffering from its popularity, puts it this way: “To reserve is to preserve.”.

Adding to the growing traffic on the trail are the effects of climate change on the Alps. Rising summer temperatures are accelerating permafrost thaw and glacier retreat, contributing to record rockfall activity in the Mont Blanc massif. While this mostly impacts the summit climbing routes, hot summers also change trail and water conditions for hikers on the Tour du Mont Blanc.

“As for the environmental impacts, trail erosion is of course the most obvious one, but we must also take into account wild bivouacking, which has multiplied, with impacts on the flora as well as the disturbance of wildlife,” claims Daniel Rodrigues, general director of the Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix, the oldest mountain guide organization in the world.

Industry observers note that “The reservation system is fair. Everyone can book their places, and tour operators can do the same. So the same rules apply to everyone, including amateur mountain consumers, and that matters to us: the mountains are a space of freedom,” claims Rodrigues. “That remarked, this space must be protected, in terms of biodiversity and environmental impacts, but also economically.”.

Industry observers note that the charter puts licensed mountain professionals at the center of safety on the trail. According to Rodrigues, that means operators will no longer be able to sell self-guided packages (just bookings and transfers) and will have to include a guide certified in all three countries.

“This is a major step forward, because the guide ensures that everyone stays safe and that everything goes smoothly. It also creates work for local people and delivers a genuine positive impact on the inhabitants of this mountain range,” adds Rodrigues.

It has been revealed that I hiked the Tour du Mont Blanc in August with Live Breathe Hike, and I came home convinced that, especially under the potential new rules, having a local guide is no longer a luxury. It’s the smartest way to hike this trail.

The TMB isn’t one trail; rather, there are a lot of different paths and detours.”There’s a classic route, but there’s a lot of different variants,” says Allison Fleece, cofounder of WHOA Travel, a women’s adventure-travel company that runs guided trips, including on the Tour du Mont Blanc. Some variants are higher and more exposed; others go along lower valleys. On our third day, instead of following the crowds, Day led us off the Col du Bonhomme on a variant toward Lac de Roselend, where we barely saw another hiker for miles. “You feel like you have the place to yourself,” says Live Breathe Hike founder Tanya Perret, who started the Chamonix-based trekking company in 2016 and says she has guided the TMB more than 75 times.

In a recent development, under the proposed rules, every night would have to be booked in advance, across three countries with different systems. Guides already do that work, and finding gems to stay at like Le Chalet de Roselend takes deep knowledge of the area. With only ten rooms, the chalet, whose balconies overlook the Lac de Roselend, was a godsend after one of our longest days of trekking. Years ago, Perret drove there to book it in person, because the elderly owner at the time only took reservations face to face. The young couple who now runs it cooks traditional dishes with local produce.

According to recent reports, the charter asks operators to buy local and partner with local producers. Good guides already do. “Many of the places that we stay are generational families, and I’ve known those families for 30 years,” notes Perret. On our trip, that meant a stop at a family cheese farm as well as the small lakeside chalet. “That’s the micro-economy,” adds Perret.

Nearly every day on my trek, Day chose a variant. Perret indicates the choice comes down to two factors: where accommodation is available and which trail will give the group the best experience that day.

It has been revealed that the variants usually turned out to be my favorite stretches. Self-guided trekkers can research the variants, but a guide knows which one fits the day. “By giving your guides a little bit of autonomy, it means they can just tweak things here and there, which makes for a unique journey,” states Perret.

Sources indicate that “The weather patterns change a lot in the mountains and they change really fast,” adds Fleece, who partners with Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix on their guided TMB trips. “Guides have years and years, most of the time decades, of experience.” A guide, she states, can help you avoid dicey situations, “but also, if you get yourself into a dicey situation, having a guide is like a safety measure to get you promptly and swiftly out of it.”.

Day has been trekking Tour Du Mont Blanc since 1992 and knows the ever-changing mountain conditions demand quick judgment. On a recent trip up Mont Blanc’s Italian route, he and his climbing partner turned back in poor snow. “We binned the whole trip,” he says. Two friends kept going, and on a ridge with snow cornices on both sides, one side broke away. “Either side could have gone,” he says.

It has been revealed that multi-day treks around the world are my favorite way to travel. With WHOA, I’ve summited Kilimanjaro and Mount Elbrus, Europe’s tallest peak (not Mont Blanc, as many assume). I’ve taken guided trips on the Trans Bhutan Trail and Japan’s Shikoku pilgrimage, which were not nearly as challenging but would have been far less rich experiences without learning the culture from our local guides. I’ve trekked the full O Trek in Patagonia without a guide, but with friends and the help of the tech giant Chile Nativo for booking refuges. Half of the O circuit, the W Trek, I hiked alone. So I know the benefits of taking guided multi-day treks and hiking alone at your own pace, stopping when you want.

Industry observers note that I can understand why travelers would want to do the TMB without a guide; many hikers do so without any issue. You can go at your own speed and take a long break for an afternoon coffee at a refuge with an open table facing the sun. A guided trip costs more. Middle options have been growing, including self-guided packages that handle the bookings for you, but even those require your due diligence and research, and could be affected by these new rules for 2027.

It has been revealed that one day on the trek, we stopped for lunch at a refuge and ran into a woman with a bandaged hand. She and her friend were on a self-guided trip whose itinerary, she told us, had started them on their first day hiking one of the route’s most exposed stretches—the ladders below Tête aux Vents—where she got injured. On the standard counterclockwise route, that section usually comes at the very end. Day told us that those ladders can easily be bypassed in busy seasons or wet weather.

It has been revealed that if you want to escape the crowds on the Tour du Mont Blanc, guides know the variants that lead to the quietest parts of the trail. Except for a few days, on certain passes, we managed to find stretches where it was just us, as far as I  could see. On our fourth day, we crossed the Col de la Seigne into Italy, past a block of granite barely knee-high: the real border marker, not the big monument nearby. I’d have walked right past it. My guide didn’t let me.

#193640. A 100-Foot Fall Stole Her Mobility. Now, Former Climbing Ranger Quinn Brett Is Rebranding Trails for Everyone.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (909 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

A 100-Foot Fall Stole Her Mobility. Now, Former Climbing Ranger Quinn Brett Is Rebranding Trails for Everyone.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey).
  • In 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park.
  • Like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quinn Brett photographed in Chasm Meadows in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Brian Watson/Jacob Bailey).

In 2017, National Park Service (NPS) climbing ranger Quinn Brett, 36, fell while ascending El Capitan in Yosemite National Park. The 120-foot drop left her paralyzed from the waist down. In a moment, she went from climbing the world’s steepest rock faces to moving in a wheelchair.

Like many Americans with mobility disabilities, Brett faced challenges when she returned to outdoor places like parklands, trail systems, and even national parks. Some of America’s wildest places were no longer accessible to her.

“To become disabled, and realize that I can’t even get across the street because there is a curb, for instance, was quite a change in perspective,” she told Climbing‘s sibling publication Outside.

According to recent reports, that’s why Brett founded the accessibility consulting firm Dovetail Trail Consulting to make outdoor spaces more accessible and usable for everyone. With her help, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) rolled out a new interactive accessibility map on October 13, connecting visitors with trails, bathrooms, and campsites that are accessible to people with mobility disabilities.

“People with disabilities don’t want to just go to the one-mile paved trail in the busiest parts of our national parks,” Brett remarked.

As part of the BLM map, visitors can snap photos of public lands and submit them, along with detailed descriptions of the infrastructure. Other users can then better understand accessibility before they hit the trail.

“You don’t have to do a construction project,” Brett said. “Just take pictures.”.

Nearly one in 10 Americans have mobility concerns, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. For these people, Brett indicates enjoying the outdoors is not just about finding the right device, but also finding trails that are made for wheels.

“For a long time we only had one pair of shoes to pick, but now with mobility device technology, we have a whole bunch of types of shoes that we get to choose from, and we want to go use our shoes in a variety of places,” Brett mentioned.

Sources indicate that kevin Oliver, chief of the BLM Division for Recreation and Business Services, participated in the three-year map project. He told Outside that the goal is to help people strategy their trip and avoid surprises from site conditions.

Sources indicate that “We’re going to continue to work to deliver more information and better information to the recreation public, so that all types of interests can be served,” Oliver told Outside. “The BLM recognizes the work is never really done. You know, we’re always perfecting it.”.

The map includes 150 existing accessible recreation opportunities. One such example is McCoy Flats in Utah, a map entry that shows the parking lot’s packed gravel, extended picnic tables, and the entrances to vault toilets.

The tool also identifies 74 additional sites where the BLM has proposed improvements. Some, like Colorado’s Blue Valley Ranch Trail, are fully funded and in progress. Others, such as New Mexico’s Glade Run Adaptive Trail, are still hunting for funding.

BLM’s fresh map is one piece of a broader push to expand trail access across federal agencies.

Sources indicate that gathering the information is only the beginning. Julia Ray, chief operating officer of the adaptability nonprofit Move United, told Outside that keeping information up to date matters just as much.

Industry observers note that “Trails are kind of living things,” Ray noted. “They change with weather and seasons, so it has to be an ongoing process to keep that information current, and where and how that information is shared is still inconsistent.”.

Industry observers note that move United partnered with Mount Rainier and Grand Canyon National Parks to assess more than 17 miles of trails for accessibility. The organization also created a free trail-access course to help local land managers understand federal accessibility standards.

Improving access at popular trails is a great way to let more people share in the national park experience, Ray stated.

“If the public go to a trail more than others, that’s probably where anybody else would want to go as well,” she remarked. “Everybody deserves the right to access the outdoors, and we are just really excited that there’s some energy around this right now.”.

For trail customers like Brett, having accessibility details means she can spend less time guessing and more time choosing where to go, what equipment to bring, and how much challenge she wants to take on. Her desire to be in the mountains hasn’t gone away, and as she claims, it never will.

Sources indicate that “I still want to be playing and going to the top of mountains and doing wild and crazy things,” Brett says. “But I also need the information to decide what experience I want.”.

In a recent development, she added that including people with disabilities in trail assessment and information gathering can help land managers identify barriers. Some mobility devices can navigate rocks, roots, and steps; a narrow bridge or gate might stop someone instead.

“Five miles of the trail might work totally fine, and then there’s a bridge to cross some water, and they just threw down a 12-inch bridge, and after that, there’s five more miles of trail that work just fine,” Brett said. “But if you’ve never hung out with somebody with a disability, then you might not know what is truly a barrier.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, some ultralight thru-hikers swear by going stoveless to save weight and time. But when you don’t cook, you might assume there are a few other things you have to do without: full flavor, fresh ingredients, and a diverse slate of nutrients, to name a few. Cold soaking—the popular method of rehydrating dry or instant food with cold water—lets you ditch the stove, fuel canister, and cook pot. But does it also have to mean compromising on a satisfying meal?

In a recent development, not necessarily. Going stoveless doesn’t have to be all cold couscous, stale chips, and stray sauce packets. Wild Planet offers ready-to-eat wild tuna bowls that are packed with protein and full of flavor. Featuring wild-caught skipjack tuna and organic ingredients, they’re a nutritious solution for anyone looking to fuel up without the fuel canister.

For the no-cook-curious, Wild Planet’s meals make for an easy transition from stove-cooked, pre-packaged backpacking meals, saving ounces while offering similar—or better—nutritional value and flavor.

Take the Wild Tuna and Red Bean Bowl, for example. It’s a tasty combination of skipjack tuna, organic beans, sweetcorn, red peppers, carrots, and spices in organic extra virgin olive oil. It offers 290 calories, with 18 grams of protein, 5 grams of fiber, and 100 milligrams of DHA omega-3s per package/serving. Each peel-and-eat package is one serving and weighs only 5.6 ounces.

It’s similar to other popular backpacking meals in both weight and nutrients per serving. But Wild Planet’s meals are ready to eat in seconds, no cooking or cold soaking required. In fact, you can bring four Wild Planet meals and still carry less than the weight of just one competing meal when combined with the weight of a typical lightweight stove, pot, and fuel. With all that weight savings, you can still add any crunchy toppings, sauces, and cheeses to boost your calorie count on major days. It’s an easy trail lunch that doesn’t compromise when it comes to flavor or nutrition.

In a recent development, it’s the combination of real, thoughtfully selected ingredients and no-prep convenience that sets Wild Planet’s meals apart. A lot of hikers go stoveless and resort to the bare essentials—“soaked quinoa plus whatever is on hand.” You can do better. When you hike with a Wild Tuna and Quinoa Bowl, you’ve got ingredients that are caught, grown, and chosen with intention. That means wild skipjack tuna, organic quinoa, delicious veggies, and gourmet spices, all sealed in organic extra virgin olive oil.

According to recent reports, hikers are naturally innovative, and with some thought, cold-soaking can deliver surprisingly elevated meals. If you want to try it for yourself, or want tips to supplement your ready-to-eat meals, here are a few basics:.

Real ingredients are always a delicious luxury in the backcountry, even for the savviest of chefs. It’s one of the appeals of Wild Planet’s tuna bowls, especially for those newly introduced to stoveless backpacking. You can just pack and peel, then pair your summit views with wild-caught tuna, whole foods, and carefully crafted flavors.

In a recent development, as a hiker, you know the importance of low-impact practices. Wild Planet believes the same. The brand prioritizes sustainable fishing practices and ocean health, and uses only pole-and-line and troll fishing methods to catch its tuna. That means hauling in only one fish per line at a time; this selective fishing has benefits for the ocean and for you.

On the environmental side, these sustainable methods are focused on preventing two of the most damaging effects of the commercial fishing industry on ocean ecosystems—overfishing and bycatch. Overfishing depletes a fish population faster than it has the chance to repopulate. Bycatch, meanwhile, occurs when non-targeted species are hauled in by accident, like sharks, sea turtles, and marine mammals like dolphins. Wild Planet’s select fishing partners don’t use nets; they monitor closely for bycatch while reeling in one fish at a time.

If you’re ready to ditch the stove for a taste of the sea, use code OUTSIDE20 to get 20% off sitewide on Wild Planet’s sustainable seafood from now until December 22. With a variety of products available to order online in convenient multipacks, you can stock up for your hiking adventures and also have quick, protein-packed meals on hand at home.

Founded in 2004, Wild Planet is the first large-scale sustainably focused canned seafood company in the U.S. Committed to protecting marine ecosystems for future generations, Wild Planet sources 100% wild-caught seafood using the highest sustainability standards, delivering nutrient-dense, minimally processed products that are as close to nature as possible. How to Make a Handprint Calendar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hanging around the house for the holidays?
  • In a recent development, we love this project because there’s no right way to make one.
  • Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by New Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

In a recent development, we love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.

It has been revealed that paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

Insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

In a recent development, now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: Latest Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids.

Print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

According to recent reports, once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

Then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.

Sleep-Unders Are Honestly a Win for Everyone

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (306 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins.
  • Industry observers note that the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part.
  • According to recent reports, all the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds.

As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins. Whether your little one wants to host a crew of first graders in your living room (hard pass) or is being asked to sleep over at someone else’s house, there are a lot of questions that come with the milestone. Will my kid have fun? Will they sleep at all? Will they be overwhelmed? Add to that concerns surrounding safety, and it’s a tough position for parents to be in. The solution: the “sleep-under.”.

Industry observers note that the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part. It’s become a trendy birthday party theme because it puts less pressure on kids and the parents hosting. How it works is that kids show up to the host house all ready for a sleepover, usually around dinner time. Guests might even arrive decked out in their coziest PJs to add to the whole sleepover vibe. The group enjoys pizza, watches a movie, plays some games, and does an activity like decorating cupcakes.

According to recent reports, all the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds. Nobody is over-tired the next day. Nobody needs to call home for a late-night pickup when they have a nightmare. No parent has to stress over whether it’s a good idea to leave their kid overnight with someone they only know from the pick-up line. No kid has to feel ashamed if they aren’t yet ready to sleep away from their parents for the night. The sleep-under side-steps all those potential problems.

According to recent reports, honestly, it’s pretty genius. We just wish it were a thing when we were kids!

#193627. Breaking: 21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1622 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tinybeans ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: 21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1622 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement.
  • Even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being.
  • In a recent development, the good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement. And while your kid’s day may be full of exploration and creativity, they can also experience a lot of anxiety, stress, and pressure. That makes it even more important to have some positive, uninterrupted time to reconnect.

Even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being. But as Randy McCoy, VP of Product & Curriculum for The Little Gym, reminds us, how long you play is less important than how often. “It’s not necessarily the ‘duration of play’ but the ‘frequency of play’ that matters most,” Mccoy says. “If a parent can give their child their undivided attention and play with them just five minutes a day, every day, they’re on the right track.”.

In a recent development, the good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep. Read on for 21 easy ideas to play with your kids, whether you have five minutes, 15, or more.

When you have a few minutes, whether it’s before school or after dinner, bust out these little-to-no-prep basics you can use just about anywhere.

1. Try out “Would You Rather?” kid edition. Spend a fun five minutes taking turns asking questions like, “Would you rather never eat ice cream again or get a trampoline?” or “Ride a dinosaur for 20 miles or an elephant for an hour?” The sillier the better. This also makes a great road trip game.

2. Make a dictionary dash. Grab a dictionary and choose a word at random. Read it out loud and have the kids guess what it means. If they can read, they can take turns finding words and trying to stump you.

3. Tickle your sidekick’s funny bone. Whip out brain busters or riddles that will make them laugh. Luckily, you don’t need Comedy Central writers for this one. We think your goofballs will get a kick out of our ultimate list of jokes for kids.

Sources indicate that 4. A few rounds of “We’re going on a picnic” alphabet-style will entertain the tot lot. The first player up claims, “I’m going on a picnic,” then adds a tasty packable to the phrase, like an apple, apricot, or avocado. Stick with ABC order or focus on just one letter for each round.

It has been revealed that 5. Play 20 questions. Have your kids guess what you’re thinking of, and keep it simple, like something you can see from where you’re standing.

6. Play a classic game of Rock, Paper, Scissors—Japanese style. It’s called Janken. Start by saying “saisho wa guu.” Then “janken pon” as you pump, before throwing on “pon.” The winning combos are still the same in this timeless, quick game you can play at home or on the go.

It has been revealed that 7. Turn yourself into a living “spot the difference” puzzle. Start with a slow model turn, then disappear and make a quick change out of sight. When you come back, your cutie’s got to spot what’s different. Did you take off a cap? Put on a scarf? Untie a shoe? Keep it easy for the tots, and kick it up a notch for older kiddos (only one earring!). Then let them have a turn trying to stump you.

Industry observers note that 8. Try out a sequencing game when the wanderlust takes hold. Name a person, place, and object, all starting with the same letter of the alphabet, then string them together like kids lining up for the school bus. “Alice from Australia loves alligators!” See how far you can get in a short amount of time.

In a recent development, for parents, playing with our kids allows us to step out of all those daily parental duties and, as McCoy explains, build friendship between parent and child. “It provides an opportunity for you to interact with them on a different level,” he says. “For a special moment, you step out of the ‘parent’ role and step into a playmate role.”  Take a break from your to-do list and try one of these 15-minute ideas that will thrill the kids and relax you, too.

Industry observers note that 9. Post-It style. A stack of Post-It notes and a pen are all it takes to play this short-and-sweet variation of the classic guessing game for parties. Choose someone to be “it.” Write on the Post-It note the name of a character from a book, movie, or show that your kid will recognize—it can be a famous person, someone they know, or a fictional character. Stick the note to their forehead, without letting them see what you wrote. Now take turns going around the room giving “it” clues to help them guess who is on their head.

10. Curl up with a good book. Putting out a basket of books in a central location motivates the kids to take a look through the pages when they’ve got time to spare. Add in a sweet bookmark that keeps track of time to make it count.

11. Give them their daily feels. Keep your favorite sensory bin fillers on hand (like cotton balls and dry beans), along with trinkets to bury and cups for spilling and filling. When you’ve got a short window, pull out the bin, fill ‘er up, and watch your kids dig and drizzle until it’s time to go.

12. Set up a quick cotton ball and straw race. Perfect for the kitchen table before lunch is served. Have siblings challenge each other for the pole position on a straightaway down the center of the table, or set up a simple obstacle course using cups that the kiddos have to work around. Ready, set, go!

13. Give a penny for their thoughts when they write in a journal. Setting aside a short amount of time to write (each day!) is a great way to encourage your amateur author’s creativity. Use silly or thought-provoking prompts to get them thinking, like, “The first time I tried …” or “When I get to be principal, I’ll …” or even “The craziest thing that happened today…” Write on, brother!

14. Give up the charade. Have your little monkey stay in character when you play a quick game of animal charades. No prep is necessary for this easy guessing game. Just pick your favorite animal and go for it! With each successful guess, trade places and start again. Ee-i-ee-i-o!

Whether your aim is active playtime or quiet(er) crafting time, filling a cool 30 minutes with your kids is easier than you think. It may take a bit of planning, but once the prep is done, it’s a sit-back-and-relax situation that’s well worth the time upfront.

15. All things LEGO. If LEGO was the first thing that popped into your head, then we’re right there with you. They’re the forever fallback for a reason, but to hit that half-hour sweet spot, try throwing a LEGO challenge into the mix: building a car that can also work underwater, or constructing a tower that’s at least 24 inches tall. Then let your master-builder go to work.

16. Spin them right round. Ana at Babble Dabble Do has a new way to play with Perler beads. She puts them to work teaching science and playing tricks when these melted beauties become spinning tops. It’s just the right amount of make-and-play to fill a brief window in your busy day.

17. One for the movers and shakers. Print out (and laminate if you’re feeling bold) The Alerting Activity Game, designed by Training Happy Hearts. Keep the deck on hand to stack the odds in your favor when the kids need something to do. With simple activities like “jump up and down ten times” or “pretend to be a volcano,” it’s packed with energy-burning activities that kids can run through on their own or with you!

18. Bring the outside in and paint it. If snow isn’t covering your yard, go for a hunt for leaves, evergreen boughs, and sticks. Then take your findings to the craft table to fancy them up with paint. Acrylics work great for this project.

For activities that span the hour, the two-step Make & Play approach works well. You may want to do a little prep the day before to make it easier, like putting crafting necessities into one small bin that you can pull out to surprise the kids.

19. Wage war. Ah, the classic card game that is so simple to learn and so hard to win. It is possible that a game of war can take longer than one hour, but it rarely takes less. You do two card battles with the highest card the winner until one person has all the cards. Get the complete rules here.

It has been revealed that 20. Create a mini catapult. Little Bins for Little Hands has an awesome tutorial, using craft sticks and other office supplies you’re sure to have around the house. Once it’s built, set up target practice plates before letting the marshmallows fly.

Recent findings suggest that 21. Put on a show. Puppets never get old; they’re easy to make with an old sock, brown paper lunch bag, or even familiar characters glued to craft sticks. Whatever method you choose, spend time creating and playing with puppets when you’ve got an hour or more to spare. Be sure to stock the craft bin with all kinds of googly eyes, buttons, yarn, and doo-dads to help bring your buddies to life. Then find an old sheet or use a baby’s blanket draped over the table to create a stage. Bravo!

It’s almost 2027, yikes! Spend an afternoon focusing on dreams and goals for the year (hello, travel!) by making a vision board with the kids. From learning a upcoming skill to going on a fantastic trip, there’s no end to the awesome things you can manifest for yourself and your family.

Mod Podge (or similar decoupaging paste).

In a recent development, if you can see your aspirations on a daily basis, they are more likely to become a reality. Start by writing down goals and ideas, and have your kids do the same!

Browse old magazines for words, phrases, and images representing each goal.

Use the Mod Podge to paste each clipped item onto the blank canvas. Be sure to brush a coat of gloss over each image. Don’t worry, it will dry clear!

Once it's done, your kids can decide where to hang or place their vision board, and remember, it should be a place they can see clearly!

Tech Report: 41 Elf on the Shelf Ideas (Because You’re Gonna Need Them)
